                    [0-24968] superscript
                      [0-24969] link: [49]
                        [0-24970] span
                          [0-19581] StaticText: [
                          [0-19582] StaticText: 49
                          [0-19583] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19584] StaticText: Thatcher told Gorbachev:
                  [0-24974] blockquote
                    [0-24975] paragraph
                      [0-19585] StaticText: We do not want a united Germany. This would lead to a change to postwar borders and we cannot allow that because such a development would undermine the stability of the whole international situation and could endanger our security.
                      [0-24976] superscript
                        [0-24977] link: [48]
                          [0-24978] span
                            [0-19586] StaticText: [
                            [0-19587] StaticText: 48
                            [0-19588] StaticText: ]
                  [0-24981] paragraph
                    [0-19589] StaticText: After the fall of the Berlin Wall, Mitterrand warned Thatcher that a unified Germany could make more ground than
                    [0-24982] link: Adolf Hitler
                    [0-19591] StaticText: ever had and that Europe would have to bear the consequences.
                    [0-24983] superscript
                      [0-24984] link: [50]
                        [0-24985] span
                          [0-19592] StaticText: [
                          [0-19593] StaticText: 50
                          [0-19594] StaticText: ]
              [0-24988] region: Legacy
                [0-24989] div
                  [0-24990] heading: Legacy
                  [0-24993] link: edit
                [0-24996] region: Celebrations and anniversaries
                  [0-24997] div
                    [0-24998] heading: Celebrations and anniversaries
                    [0-25001] link: edit
                  [0-25004] paragraph
                    [0-19603] StaticText: On 21 November 1989,
                    [0-25005] link: Crosby, Stills & Nash
                    [0-19605] StaticText: performed the song "Chippin' Away" from
                    [0-25006] link: Graham Nash
                    [0-19607] StaticText: 's 1986 solo album
                    [0-25008] link: Innocent Eyes
                    [0-19609] StaticText: in front of the Brandenburg Gate.
                    [0-25009] superscript
                      [0-25010] link: [51]
                        [0-25011] span
                          [0-19610] StaticText: [
                          [0-19611] StaticText: 51
                          [0-19612] StaticText: ]
                  [0-25014] paragraph
                    [0-19613] StaticText: On 25 December 1989,
                    [0-25015] link: Leonard Bernstein
                    [0-19615] StaticText: gave a concert in Berlin celebrating the end of the Wall, including
                    [0-25016] link: Beethoven's
                    [0-19617] StaticText: 
                    [0-25017] link: 9th symphony
                    [0-19619] StaticText: (
                    [0-25019] link: Ode to Joy
                    [0-19621] StaticText: ) with the word "Joy"
                    [0-25020] i
                      [0-19622] StaticText: (
                      [0-19623] StaticText: Freude
                      [0-19624] StaticText: )
                    [0-19625] StaticText: changed to "Freedom"
                    [0-25024] i
                      [0-19626] StaticText: (
                      [0-19627] StaticText: Freiheit
                      [0-19628] StaticText: )
                    [0-19629] StaticText: in the lyrics sung. The poet
                    [0-25028] link: Schiller
                    [0-19631] StaticText: may have originally written "Freedom" and changed it to "Joy" out of fear. The orchestra and choir were drawn from both East and West Germany, as well as the United Kingdom, France, the Soviet Union, and the United States.
                    [0-25029] superscript
                      [0-25030] link: [52]
                        [0-25031] span
                          [0-19632] StaticText: [
                          [0-19633] StaticText: 52
                          [0-19634] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19635] StaticText: On New Year's Eve 1989,
                    [0-25034] link: David Hasselhoff
                    [0-19637] StaticText: performed his song "
                    [0-25035] link: Looking for Freedom
                    [0-19639] StaticText: " while standing atop the partly demolished Wall in front of 200,000 people.
                    [0-25036] superscript
                      [0-25037] link: [53]
                        [0-25038] span
                          [0-19640] StaticText: [
                          [0-19641] StaticText: 53
                          [0-19642] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19643] StaticText: 
                    [0-25041] link: Roger Waters
                    [0-19645] StaticText: 
                    [0-25042] link: performed
                    [0-19647] StaticText: the
                    [0-25043] link: Pink Floyd
                    [0-19649] StaticText: album
                    [0-25045] link: The Wall
                    [0-19651] StaticText: just north of
                    [0-25046] link: Potsdamer Platz
                    [0-19653] StaticText: on 21 July 1990, with guests including
                    [0-25047] link: Scorpions
                    [0-19655] StaticText: ,
                    [0-25048] link: Bryan Adams
                    [0-19657] StaticText: ,
                    [0-25049] link: Sinéad O'Connor
                    [0-19659] StaticText: ,
                    [0-25050] link: Cyndi Lauper
                    [0-19661] StaticText: ,
                    [0-25051] link: Thomas Dolby
                    [0-19663] StaticText: ,
                    [0-25052] link: Joni Mitchell
                    [0-19665] StaticText: ,
                    [0-25053] link: Marianne Faithfull
                    [0-19667] StaticText: ,
                    [0-25054] link: Levon Helm
                    [0-19669] StaticText: ,
                    [0-25055] link: Rick Danko
                    [0-19671] StaticText: and
                    [0-25056] link: Van Morrison
                    [0-19673] StaticText: .
                    [0-25057] superscript
                      [0-25058] link: [54]
                        [0-25059] span
                          [0-19674] StaticText: [
                          [0-19675] StaticText: 54
                          [0-19676] StaticText: ]
                  [0-25062] paragraph
                    [0-19677] StaticText: Over the years, there has been a repeated controversial debate
                    [0-25063] superscript
                      [0-25064] link: [55]
                        [0-25065] span
                          [0-19678] StaticText: [
                          [0-19679] StaticText: 55
                          [0-19680] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19681] StaticText: as to whether
                    [0-25068] link: 9 November
                    [0-19683] StaticText: would make a suitable German national holiday, often initiated by former members of political opposition in East Germany, such as
                    [0-25069] link: Werner Schulz
                    [0-19685] StaticText: .
                    [0-25070] superscript
                      [0-25071] link: [56]
                        [0-25072] span
                          [0-19686] StaticText: [
                          [0-19687] StaticText: 56
                          [0-19688] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19689] StaticText: Besides being the emotional apogee of East Germany's peaceful revolution, 9 November is also the date of the 1918 abdication of Kaiser
                    [0-25075] link: Wilhelm II
                    [0-19691] StaticText: and declaration of the
                    [0-25076] link: Weimar Republic
                    [0-19693] StaticText: , the first German republic. However, 9 November is also the anniversary of the execution of
                    [0-25077] link: Robert Blum
                    [0-19695] StaticText: following the
                    [0-25078] link: 1848 Vienna revolts
                    [0-19697] StaticText: , the 1923
                    [0-25079] link: Beer Hall Putsch
                    [0-19699] StaticText: , and the infamous
                    [0-25081] link: Kristallnacht
                    [0-19701] StaticText: 
                    [0-25082] link: pogroms
                    [0-19703] StaticText: of the Nazis in 1938.
                    [0-25083] link: Nobel
                    [0-19705] StaticText: Laureate
                    [0-25084] link: Elie Wiesel
                    [0-19707] StaticText: criticised the first euphoria, noting that "they forgot that 9 November has already entered into history—51 years earlier it marked the Kristallnacht."
                    [0-25085] superscript
                      [0-25086] link: [57]
                        [0-25087] span
                          [0-19708] StaticText: [
                          [0-19709] StaticText: 57
                          [0-19710] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19711] StaticText: As reunification was not official and complete until 3 October (1990), that day was finally chosen as
                    [0-25090] link: German Unity Day
                    [0-19713] StaticText: .
                  [0-25091] region: 10th anniversary celebrations
                    [0-25092] div
                      [0-25093] heading: 10th anniversary celebrations
                      [0-25096] link: edit
                    [0-25099] paragraph
                      [0-19718] StaticText: On 9 November 1999, the 10th anniversary was observed with a concert and fireworks at the
                      [0-25100] link: Brandenburg Gate
                      [0-19720] StaticText: . Russian cellist
                      [0-25101] link: Mstislav Rostropovich
                      [0-19722] StaticText: played music by
                      [0-25102] link: Johann Sebastian Bach
                      [0-19724] StaticText: , while German rock band
                      [0-25103] link: Scorpions
                      [0-19726] StaticText: performed their 1990 song
                      [0-25105] link: Wind of Change
                      [0-19728] StaticText: . Wreaths were placed for victims shot down when they
                      [0-25106] link: attempted to escape to the west
                      [0-19730] StaticText: , and politicians delivered speeches.
                      [0-25107] superscript
                        [0-25108] link: [58]
                          [0-25109] span
                            [0-19731] StaticText: [
                            [0-19732] StaticText: 58
                            [0-19733] StaticText: ]
                      [0-25112] superscript
                        [0-25113] link: [59]
                          [0-25114] span
                            [0-19734] StaticText: [
                            [0-19735] StaticText: 59
                            [0-19736] StaticText: ]
                  [0-25117] region: 20th anniversary celebrations
                    [0-25118] div
                      [0-25119] heading: 20th anniversary celebrations
                      [0-25122] link: edit
                    [0-25125] paragraph
                      [0-19741] StaticText: On 9 November 2009, Berlin celebrated the 20th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall with a "Festival of Freedom" with dignitaries from around the world in attendance for an evening celebration around the Brandenburg Gate. A high point was when over 1,000 colourfully designed foam domino tiles, each over
                      [0-19742] StaticText: 8 feet (2.4
                      [0-19743] StaticText: 
                      [0-19744] StaticText: m)
                      [0-19745] StaticText: tall, that were stacked along the former route of the Wall in the city center were toppled in stages, converging in front of the Brandenburg Gate.
                      [0-25129] superscript
                        [0-25130] link: [60]
                          [0-25131] span
                            [0-19746] StaticText: [
                            [0-19747] StaticText: 60
                            [0-19748] StaticText: ]
                    [0-25134] paragraph
                      [0-19749] StaticText: A Berlin Twitter Wall was set up to allow Twitter users to post messages commemorating the 20th anniversary. The
                      [0-25135] link: Chinese government
                      [0-19751] StaticText: quickly shut down access to the Twitter Wall after internet users in China began using it to protest the
                      [0-25136] link: Great Firewall
                      [0-19753] StaticText: .
                      [0-25137] superscript
                        [0-25138] link: [61]
                          [0-25139] span
                            [0-19754] StaticText: [
                            [0-19755] StaticText: 61
                            [0-19756] StaticText: ]
                      [0-25142] superscript
                        [0-25143] link: [62]
                          [0-25144] span
                            [0-19757] StaticText: [
                            [0-19758] StaticText: 62
                            [0-19759] StaticText: ]
                      [0-25147] superscript
                        [0-25148] link: [63]
                          [0-25149] span
                            [0-19760] StaticText: [
                            [0-19761] StaticText: 63
                            [0-19762] StaticText: ]
                    [0-25152] paragraph
                      [0-19763] StaticText: In the United States, the German Embassy coordinated a public diplomacy campaign with the motto "Freedom Without Walls", to commemorate the 20th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall. The campaign was focused on promoting awareness of the fall of the Berlin Wall among current college students. Students at over 30 universities participated in "Freedom Without Walls" events in late 2009. First place winner of the Freedom Without Walls Speaking Contest
                      [0-25153] superscript
                        [0-25154] link: [64]
                          [0-25155] span
                            [0-19764] StaticText: [
                            [0-19765] StaticText: 64
                            [0-19766] StaticText: ]
                      [0-19767] StaticText: Robert Cannon received a free trip to Berlin for 2010.
                      [0-25158] superscript
                        [0-25159] link: [65]
                          [0-25160] span
                            [0-19768] StaticText: [
                            [0-19769] StaticText: 65
                            [0-19770] StaticText: ]
                    [0-25163] paragraph
                      [0-19771] StaticText: An international project called
                      [0-19772] StaticText: Mauerreise
                      [0-19773] StaticText: (Journey of the Wall) took place in various countries. Twenty symbolic Wall bricks were sent from Berlin starting in May 2009, with the destinations being Korea, Cyprus, Yemen, and other places where everyday life is characterised by division and border experience. In these places, the bricks would become a blank canvas for artists, intellectuals and young people to tackle the "Wall" phenomenon.
                      [0-25165] superscript
                        [0-25166] link: [66]
                          [0-25167] span
                            [0-19774] StaticText: [
                            [0-19775] StaticText: 66
                            [0-19776] StaticText: ]
                    [0-25170] paragraph
                      [0-19777] StaticText: To commemorate the 20th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall, the 3D online virtual world
                      [0-25172] link: Twinity
                      [0-19779] StaticText: reconstructed a true-to-scale section of the Wall in virtual Berlin.
                      [0-25173] superscript
                        [0-25174] link: [67]
                          [0-25175] span
                            [0-19780] StaticText: [
                            [0-19781] StaticText: 67
                            [0-19782] StaticText: ]
                      [0-19783] StaticText: The
                      [0-25178] link: MTV Europe Music Awards
                      [0-19785] StaticText: , on 5 November, had
                      [0-25179] link: U2
                      [0-19787] StaticText: and
                      [0-25180] link: Tokio Hotel
                      [0-19789] StaticText: perform songs dedicated to and about the Berlin Wall. U2 performed at the Brandenburg Gate, and Tokio Hotel performed "
                      [0-25181] link: World Behind My Wall
                      [0-19791] StaticText: ".
                    [0-25182] paragraph
                      [0-25183] link: Palestinians
                      [0-19793] StaticText: in the town of
                      [0-25184] link: Kalandia
                      [0-19795] StaticText: ,
                      [0-25185] link: West Bank
                      [0-19797] StaticText: , pulled down parts of the
                      [0-25186] link: Israeli West Bank barrier
                      [0-19799] StaticText: , in a demonstration marking the 20th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall.
                      [0-25187] superscript
                        [0-25188] link: [68]
                          [0-25189] span
                            [0-19800] StaticText: [
                            [0-19801] StaticText: 68
                            [0-19802] StaticText: ]
                    [0-25192] paragraph
                      [0-19803] StaticText: The
                      [0-25193] link: International Spy Museum
                      [0-19805] StaticText: in Washington D.C., hosted a
                      [0-25194] link: Trabant
                      [0-19807] StaticText: car rally where 20 Trabants gathered in recognition of the 20th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall. Rides were raffled every half-hour and a Trabant crashed through a Berlin Wall mock up. The Trabant was the East German people's car that many used to leave DDR after the collapse.
                      [0-25195] superscript
                        [0-25196] link: [69]
                          [0-25197] span
                            [0-19808] StaticText: [
                            [0-19809] StaticText: 69
                            [0-19810] StaticText: ]
                      [0-25200] superscript
                        [0-25201] link: [70]
                          [0-25202] span
                            [0-19811] StaticText: [
                            [0-19812] StaticText: 70
                            [0-19813] StaticText: ]
                    [0-25205] paragraph
                      [0-19814] StaticText: The
                      [0-25206] link: Allied Museum
                      [0-19816] StaticText: in the
                      [0-25207] link: Dahlem
                      [0-19818] StaticText: district of Berlin hosted a number of events to mark the 20th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall. The museum held a Special Exhibition entitled "Wall Patrol – The Western Powers and the Berlin Wall 1961–1990" which focused on the daily patrols deployed by the Western powers to observe the situation along the Berlin Wall and the fortifications on the
                      [0-25208] link: GDR
                      [0-19820] StaticText: 
                      [0-25209] link: border
                      [0-19822] StaticText: .
                      [0-25210] superscript
                        [0-25211] link: [71]
                          [0-25212] span
                            [0-19823] StaticText: [
                            [0-19824] StaticText: 71
                            [0-19825] StaticText: ]
                      [0-19826] StaticText: A sheet of "Americans in Berlin" Commemorative
                      [0-25215] link: Cinderella stamps
                      [0-19828] StaticText: designed by
                      [0-25216] link: T.H.E. Hill
                      [0-19830] StaticText: was presented to the Museum by David Guerra, Berlin veteran and webmaster of the site
                      [0-25217] link: www.berlinbrigade.com
                      [0-19832] StaticText: .

                        [0-25219] link: [72]
                          [0-25220] span
                            [0-19833] StaticText: [
                            [0-19834] StaticText: 72

                  [0-25223] region: 30th anniversary celebrations
                    [0-25224] div
                      [0-25225] heading: 30th anniversary celebrations
                      [0-25228] link: edit
                    [0-25231] paragraph
                      [0-19840] StaticText: Berlin planned a week-long arts festival from 4 to 10 November 2019 and a citywide music festival on 9 November to celebrate the 30th anniversary.
                      [0-25232] superscript
                        [0-25233] link: [73]
                          [0-25234] span
                            [0-19841] StaticText: [
                            [0-19842] StaticText: 73
                            [0-19843] StaticText: ]
                      [0-25237] superscript
                        [0-25238] link: [74]
                          [0-25239] span
                            [0-19844] StaticText: [
                            [0-19845] StaticText: 74
                            [0-19846] StaticText: ]
                      [0-19847] StaticText: On 4 November, outdoor exhibits opened at Alexanderplatz, the Brandenburg Gate, the East Side Gallery, Gethsemane Church, Kurfürstendamm, Schlossplatz, and the former Stasi headquarters in Lichtenberg.
                      [0-25242] superscript
                        [0-25243] link: [74]
                          [0-25244] span
                            [0-19848] StaticText: [
                            [0-19849] StaticText: 74
                            [0-19850] StaticText: ]
                [0-25247] region: Polling
                  [0-25248] div
                    [0-25249] heading: Polling
                    [0-25252] link: edit
                  [0-25257] note
                    [0-19855] StaticText: Further information:
                    [0-25258] link: Ostalgie
                  [0-25259] paragraph
                    [0-19857] StaticText: A small minority still support the wall or even support rebuilding the wall back up. A 2008 poll found that 11% of participants from the former West Berlin and 12% from the former East Berlin said it would be better if the wall was still in place.
                    [0-25260] superscript
                      [0-25261] link: [75]
                        [0-25262] span
                          [0-19858] StaticText: [
                          [0-19859] StaticText: 75
                          [0-19860] StaticText: ]
                  [0-25265] paragraph
                    [0-19861] StaticText: A November 2009 poll found that 12% of Germans said the wall should be rebuilt. The poll also found that in the former
                    [0-25266] link: West German states
                    [0-19863] StaticText: support was at 12% and in the former
                    [0-25267] link: East German states
                    [0-19865] StaticText: it was 13%. A September 2009 poll found 15% of Germans supported a wall, while in the west it was 16% and in the east it was at 10%.
                    [0-25268] superscript
                      [0-25269] link: [76]
                        [0-25270] span
                          [0-19866] StaticText: [
                          [0-19867] StaticText: 76
                          [0-19868] StaticText: ]
                    [0-25273] superscript
                      [0-25274] link: [77]
                        [0-25275] span
                          [0-19869] StaticText: [
                          [0-19870] StaticText: 77
                          [0-19871] StaticText: ]
                  [0-25278] paragraph
                    [0-19872] StaticText: A 2010 poll from Emnid for
                    [0-25280] link: Bild
                    [0-19874] StaticText: found that 24% of West Germans and 23% of East Germans wished for the wall to remain.
                    [0-25281] superscript
                      [0-25282] link: [78]
                        [0-25283] span
                          [0-19875] StaticText: [
                          [0-19876] StaticText: 78
                          [0-19877] StaticText: ]
                    [0-25286] superscript
                      [0-25287] link: [79]
                        [0-25288] span
                          [0-19878] StaticText: [
                          [0-19879] StaticText: 79
                          [0-19880] StaticText: ]
                    [0-25291] superscript
                      [0-25292] link: [80]
                        [0-25293] span
                          [0-19881] StaticText: [
                          [0-19882] StaticText: 80
                          [0-19883] StaticText: ]
                    [0-25296] superscript
                      [0-25297] link: [81]
                        [0-25298] span
                          [0-19884] StaticText: [
                          [0-19885] StaticText: 81
                          [0-19886] StaticText: ]
                  [0-25301] paragraph
                    [0-19887] StaticText: A 2011 poll from
                    [0-25303] link: Berliner Zeitung
                    [0-19889] StaticText: on the 30th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall found that 8% of Berliners opposed the fall, while 87% supported the fall. The poll also found that 28% of
                    [0-25304] link: Alternative for Germany
                    [0-19891] StaticText: (AfD) and 16% of
                    [0-25305] link: Free Democratic Party
                    [0-19893] StaticText: (FDP) supporters supported bringing back the wall.
                    [0-25306] superscript
                      [0-25307] link: [82]
                        [0-25308] span
                          [0-19894] StaticText: [
                          [0-19895] StaticText: 82
                          [0-19896] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19897] StaticText: A 2019 Yougov poll found that 13% of Germans wanted the wall back; in the West support was at 14%, and in the East it was 13%.
                    [0-25311] superscript
                      [0-23068] link: [83]
                        [0-25312] span
                          [0-19898] StaticText: [
                          [0-19899] StaticText: 83
                          [0-19900] StaticText: ]
                  [0-25315] paragraph
                    [0-19901] StaticText: A 2019 poll from
                    [0-25316] link: Forsa
                    [0-19903] StaticText: found 35% of Berliners thought the construction of the wall was not bad, with supporters of
                    [0-25317] link: Die Linke
                    [0-19905] StaticText: at 74%.

                [0-23892] paragraph
                  [0-18817] StaticText: The
                  [0-23893] b
                    [0-18818] StaticText: Fall of the
                    [0-23894] link: Berlin Wall
                  [0-18820] StaticText: and the
                  [0-23896] link: fortified inner German border
                  [0-18822] StaticText: occurred
                  [0-18823] StaticText: immediately... without delay
                  [0-18824] StaticText: after a
                  [0-23898] link: Politburo
                  [0-18826] StaticText: press conference on
                  [0-23899] link: 9 November
                  [0-18828] StaticText: 1989 prematurely announced that
                  [0-23900] link: East Germans
                  [0-18830] StaticText: could travel without restrictions after, in the decades before, hundreds had been killed by
                  [0-23901] link: Border Troops of the German Democratic Republic
                  [0-18832] StaticText: when trying to sneak through the
                  [0-23902] link: Iron Curtain
                  [0-18834] StaticText: .
                [0-23903] paragraph
                  [0-18835] StaticText: Soon, people gathered at
                  [0-23904] link: Berlin border crossings
                  [0-18837] StaticText: , citing the news that were broadcast in East and West, and puzzled border guards eventually let them pass in the late evening hours, with live television broadcasting worldwide. The next days, thousands travelled across the border, also in other places less covered by press. After this symbolic fall, obstacles were removed, former crossings were opened again, and following
                  [0-23905] link: demolition
                  [0-18839] StaticText: ,
                  [0-23906] link: L-shaped concrete segments of the Berlin wall
                  [0-18841] StaticText: were actually falling
                  [0-23907] superscript
                    [0-23908] link: [2]
                      [0-23909] span
                        [0-18842] StaticText: [
                        [0-18843] StaticText: 2
                        [0-18844] StaticText: ]
                  [0-18845] StaticText: and spread around the world.
                [0-23912] paragraph
                  [0-18846] StaticText: In the early stages of the
                  [0-23913] link: Revolutions of 1989
                  [0-18848] StaticText: , Hungary
                  [0-23914] link: removed the fence
                  [0-18850] StaticText: in May and
                  [0-23915] link: opened its border
                  [0-18852] StaticText: in August, and after many East German families had fled into the
                  [0-23916] link: West German embassy in Prague
                  [0-18854] StaticText: , the
                  [0-23917] link: CSSR
                  [0-18856] StaticText: followed in late September. Despite holiday season being over, East Germans continued to defect via neighbouring
                  [0-23918] link: Communist Bloc
                  [0-18858] StaticText: countries, putting pressure on the East German leaders to either shut down these borders, too, or "letting steam off" by allowing disgruntled citizens to directly emigrate to West Germany. Long-term leader
                  [0-23919] link: Erich Honecker
                  [0-18860] StaticText: was ousted in October, and while new communist leaders discussed a travel law, the premature publication led to a total loss of control over the formerly fortified, lethal border, and due to the ensuing
                  [0-23920] link: Peaceful Revolution
                  [0-18862] StaticText: , over the country itself. After the
                  [0-23921] link: first free elections in spring 1990
                  [0-18864] StaticText: showed preference for a
                  [0-23922] link: German reunification
                  [0-18866] StaticText: and for the Western
                  [0-23923] link: Deutsche Mark
                  [0-18868] StaticText: . The DM already came in July, unification took place on 3 October 1990 when
                  [0-23924] link: 5 new states
                  [0-18870] StaticText: joined the
                  [0-23925] link: 10 old states
                  [0-18872] StaticText: of the
                  [0-23926] link: Federal Republic of Germany
                  [0-18874] StaticText: , with reunited Berlin being a 16th state.
                  [0-23927] link: Soviet occupation forces
                  [0-18876] StaticText: left until 1994.

                    [0-18881] StaticText: In Berlin, East Germans in their little

                  [0-23960] paragraph
                    [0-18899] StaticText: The June
                    [0-23961] link: 1989 Tiananmen Square protests and massacre
                    [0-18901] StaticText: had shown what could happen under communist rule. The opening of the
                    [0-23962] link: Iron Curtain
                    [0-18903] StaticText: between Austria and Hungary at the
                    [0-23963] link: Pan-European Picnic
                    [0-18905] StaticText: on 19 August 1989 set in motion a peaceful chain reaction, at the end of which there was no longer an
                    [0-23964] link: East Germany
                    [0-18907] StaticText: and the
                    [0-23965] link: Eastern Bloc
                    [0-18909] StaticText: had disintegrated.
                  [0-23966] paragraph
                    [0-18910] StaticText: After the picnic, which was based on an idea by
                    [0-23967] link: Otto von Habsburg
                    [0-18912] StaticText: to test the reaction of the
                    [0-23968] link: USSR
                    [0-18914] StaticText: and
                    [0-23078] link: Mikhail Gorbachev
                    [0-18916] StaticText: to an opening of the border, tens of thousands of media-informed East Germans set off for Hungary.
                    [0-23969] link: Erich Honecker
                    [0-18918] StaticText: dictated to the
                    [0-18919] StaticText: Daily Mirror
                    [0-18920] StaticText: for the Pan-European Picnic:
                    [0-23971] i
                      [0-18921] StaticText: "Habsburg distributed leaflets far into Poland, on which the East German holidaymakers were invited to a picnic. When they came to the picnic, they were given gifts, food and
                      [0-23972] link: Deutsche Mark
                      [0-18923] StaticText: , and then they were persuaded to come to the West."
                    [0-18924] StaticText: The leadership of the GDR in East Berlin did not dare to completely block the borders to their
                    [0-23973] link: "socialist brother lands"

                    [0-18945] StaticText: Following the summer of 1989, by early November refugees were finding their way to

                    [0-24006] link: West German embassy in Prague
                    [0-18949] StaticText: . On 30 September, following negotiations with East Germany and the Soviet Union, the West German
                    [0-24007] link: Foreign Minister
                    [0-18951] StaticText: 
                    [0-24008] link: Hans-Dietrich Genscher
                    [0-18953] StaticText: went to the Prague embassy to personally inform the thousands of refugees that they were allowed to leave for West Germany. His speech from the embassy's balcony was drowned out after the line
                    [0-18954] StaticText: "Wir sind zu Ihnen gekommen, um Ihnen mitzuteilen, dass heute Ihre Ausreise..."

However, this movement of people grew so large it caused difficulties for both countries. In addition, East Germany was struggling to meet loan payments on foreign borrowings;

                  [0-23918] link: Communist Bloc
                  [0-18858] StaticText: countries, putting pressure on the East German leaders to either shut down these borders, too, or "letting steam off" by allowing disgruntled citizens to directly emigrate to West Germany. Long-term leader
                  [0-23919] link: Erich Honecker
                  [0-18860] StaticText: was ousted in October, and while new communist leaders discussed a travel law, the premature publication led to a total loss of control over the formerly fortified, lethal border, and due to the ensuing
                  [0-23920] link: Peaceful Revolution
                  [0-18862] StaticText: , over the country itself. After the
                  [0-23921] link: first free elections in spring 1990
                  [0-18864] StaticText: showed preference for a
                  [0-23922] link: German reunification
                  [0-18866] StaticText: and for the Western
                  [0-23923] link: Deutsche Mark
                  [0-18868] StaticText: . The DM already came in July, unification took place on 3 October 1990 when
                  [0-23924] link: 5 new states
                  [0-18870] StaticText: joined the
                  [0-23925] link: 10 old states
                  [0-18872] StaticText: of the
                  [0-23926] link: Federal Republic of Germany
                  [0-18874] StaticText: , with reunited Berlin being a 16th state.
                  [0-23927] link: Soviet occupation forces
                  [0-18876] StaticText: left until 1994.
              [0-23929] region: Background
                [0-23930] div
                  [0-23931] heading: Background
                  [0-23934] link: edit
                [0-23937] figure
                  [0-23938] link
                    [0-23063] image
                  [0-23939] Figcaption
                    [0-18881] StaticText: In Berlin, East Germans in their little
                    [0-23940] link: Trabant cars
                    [0-18883] StaticText: are greeted by West Germans carrying a "Test the
                    [0-23941] link: West
                    [0-18885] StaticText: " banner, citing a cigarette ad slogan
                [0-23942] region: Opening of the Iron Curtain
                  [0-23943] div
                    [0-23944] heading: Opening of the Iron Curtain
                    [0-23947] link: edit
                  [0-23950] figure
                    [0-23951] link
                      [0-23061] image
                    [0-23952] Figcaption
                      [0-18890] StaticText: This section of the Wall's "death strip" in 1977 featured
                      [0-23953] link: Czech hedgehogs
                      [0-18892] StaticText: , a
                      [0-23954] link: guard tower
                      [0-18894] StaticText: and a cleared area
                  [0-23957] note
                    [0-18895] StaticText: Further information:
                    [0-23958] link: Pan-European Picnic
                    [0-18897] StaticText: and
                    [0-23959] link: Removal of Hungary's border fence with Austria
                  [0-23960] paragraph
                    [0-18899] StaticText: The June
                    [0-23961] link: 1989 Tiananmen Square protests and massacre
                    [0-18901] StaticText: had shown what could happen under communist rule. The opening of the
                    [0-23962] link: Iron Curtain
                    [0-18903] StaticText: between Austria and Hungary at the
                    [0-23963] link: Pan-European Picnic
                    [0-18905] StaticText: on 19 August 1989 set in motion a peaceful chain reaction, at the end of which there was no longer an
                    [0-23964] link: East Germany
                    [0-18907] StaticText: and the
                    [0-23965] link: Eastern Bloc
                    [0-18909] StaticText: had disintegrated.
                  [0-23966] paragraph
                    [0-18910] StaticText: After the picnic, which was based on an idea by
                    [0-23967] link: Otto von Habsburg
                    [0-18912] StaticText: to test the reaction of the
                    [0-23968] link: USSR
                    [0-18914] StaticText: and
                    [0-23078] link: Mikhail Gorbachev
                    [0-18916] StaticText: to an opening of the border, tens of thousands of media-informed East Germans set off for Hungary.
                    [0-23969] link: Erich Honecker
                    [0-18918] StaticText: dictated to the
                    [0-18919] StaticText: Daily Mirror
                    [0-18920] StaticText: for the Pan-European Picnic:
                    [0-23971] i
                      [0-18921] StaticText: "Habsburg distributed leaflets far into Poland, on which the East German holidaymakers were invited to a picnic. When they came to the picnic, they were given gifts, food and
                      [0-23972] link: Deutsche Mark
                      [0-18923] StaticText: , and then they were persuaded to come to the West."
                    [0-18924] StaticText: The leadership of the GDR in East Berlin did not dare to completely block the borders to their
                    [0-23973] link: "socialist brother lands"
                    [0-18926] StaticText: , and the USSR did not respond at all. Thus the bracket of the Eastern Bloc was broken.
                    [0-23974] superscript
                      [0-23975] link: [3]

                    [0-23999] superscript
                      [0-24000] link: [8]
                        [0-24001] span

                          [0-18943] StaticText: 8
                          [0-18944] StaticText: ]
                  [0-24004] paragraph
                    [0-18945] StaticText: Following the summer of 1989, by early November refugees were finding their way to
                    [0-24005] link: Hungary
                    [0-18947] StaticText: via Czechoslovakia or via the
                    [0-24006] link: West German embassy in Prague
                    [0-18949] StaticText: . On 30 September, following negotiations with East Germany and the Soviet Union, the West German
                    [0-24007] link: Foreign Minister
                    [0-18951] StaticText: 
                    [0-24008] link: Hans-Dietrich Genscher
                    [0-18953] StaticText: went to the Prague embassy to personally inform the thousands of refugees that they were allowed to leave for West Germany. His speech from the embassy's balcony was drowned out after the line
                    [0-18954] StaticText: "Wir sind zu Ihnen gekommen, um Ihnen mitzuteilen, dass heute Ihre Ausreise..."
                    [0-18955] StaticText: ("We came to you, to let you know that today, your departure...") was met with loud cheers and jubilations. The next day, the first of the embassy refugees left
                    [0-24010] link: Prague
                    [0-18957] StaticText: via a train ride through the GDR for
                    [0-24011] link: Bavaria
                    [0-18959] StaticText: .
                    [0-24012] superscript
                      [0-24013] link: [9]
                        [0-24014] span
                          [0-18960] StaticText: [
                          [0-18961] StaticText: 9
                          [0-18962] StaticText: ]
                    [0-24017] superscript
                      [0-24018] link: [10]
                        [0-24019] span
                          [0-18963] StaticText: [
                          [0-18964] StaticText: 10
                          [0-18965] StaticText: ]
                  [0-24022] paragraph
                    [0-18966] StaticText: The emigration was initially tolerated because of long-standing agreements with the communist Czechoslovak government, allowing free travel across their common border. However, this movement of people grew so large it caused difficulties for both countries. In addition, East Germany was struggling to meet loan payments on foreign borrowings;
                    [0-24023] link: Egon Krenz
                    [0-18968] StaticText: sent
                    [0-24024] link: Alexander Schalck-Golodkowski
                    [0-18970] StaticText: to unsuccessfully ask West Germany for a short-term loan to make interest payments.
                    [0-24025] superscript
                      [0-24026] link: [11]
                        [0-24027] span
                          [0-18971] StaticText: [
                          [0-18972] StaticText: 11
                          [0-18973] StaticText: ]

                        [0-18976] StaticText: 344
                        [0-18977] StaticText: 
                [0-24035] region: Protection of the wall
                  [0-24036] div
                    [0-24037] heading: Protection of the wall
                    [0-24040] link: edit
                  [0-24043] paragraph
                    [0-18982] StaticText: The Berlin Wall, officially the "
                    [0-24044] link: Anti-fascist protection wall
                    [0-18984] StaticText: ", was made up of two concrete walls, one facing the West and covered with graffiti. Both walls were 4 metres tall and had a length of 155 kilometres. They were separated by a mined corridor called the
                    [0-24045] link: death strip
                    [0-18986] StaticText: . This strip was heavily guarded and included 302 watchtowers (by 1989). Guards had authorization to shoot people who attempted to go through this strip.
                    [0-24046] superscript
                      [0-24047] link: [12]
                        [0-24048] span
                          [0-18987] StaticText: [
                          [0-18988] StaticText: 12
                          [0-18989] StaticText: ]
                    [0-24051] superscript
                      [0-24052] link: [13]
                        [0-24053] span
                          [0-18990] StaticText: [
                          [0-18991] StaticText: 13
                          [0-18992] StaticText: ]
                [0-24056] region: Political changes in East Germany
                  [0-24057] div
                    [0-24058] heading: Political changes in East Germany
                    [0-24061] link: edit
                  [0-24064] paragraph
                    [0-18997] StaticText: On 18 October 1989, longtime
                    [0-24065] link: Socialist Unity Party of Germany
                    [0-18999] StaticText: (SED) leader
                    [0-24066] link: Erich Honecker
                    [0-19001] StaticText: stepped down in favor of Krenz. Honecker had been seriously ill, and those looking to replace him were initially willing to wait for a "biological solution", but by October were convinced that the political and economic situation was too grave.
                    [0-24067] superscript
                      [0-24068] link: [11]
                        [0-24069] span
                          [0-19002] StaticText: [
                          [0-19003] StaticText: 11
                          [0-19004] StaticText: ]
                    [0-24072] superscript
                      [0-24073] span
                        [0-19005] StaticText: :
                        [0-19006] StaticText: 
                        [0-19007] StaticText: 339
                        [0-19008] StaticText: 
                    [0-19009] StaticText: Honecker approved the choice, naming Krenz in his resignation speech,
                    [0-24077] superscript
                      [0-24078] link: [14]
                        [0-24079] span
                          [0-19010] StaticText: [
                          [0-19011] StaticText: 14
                          [0-19012] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19013] StaticText: and the
                    [0-24082] link: Volkskammer
                    [0-19015] StaticText: duly elected him. Although Krenz promised reforms in his first public speech,
                    [0-24083] superscript
                      [0-24084] link: [15]
                        [0-24085] span
                          [0-19016] StaticText: [
                          [0-19017] StaticText: 15
                          [0-19018] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19019] StaticText: he was considered by the East German public to be following his predecessor's policies, and public protests demanding his resignation continued.
                    [0-24088] superscript
                      [0-23069] link: [11]
                        [0-24089] span
                          [0-19020] StaticText: [
                          [0-19021] StaticText: 11
                          [0-19022] StaticText: ]
                    [0-24092] superscript
                      [0-24093] span
                        [0-19023] StaticText: :
                        [0-19024] StaticText: 
                        [0-19025] StaticText: 347
                        [0-19026] StaticText: 
                    [0-19027] StaticText: Despite promises of reform, public opposition to the regime continued to grow.
                  [0-24097] paragraph
                    [0-19028] StaticText: On 1 November, Krenz authorized the reopening of the border with
                    [0-24098] link: Czechoslovakia
                    [0-19030] StaticText: , which had been sealed to prevent East Germans from fleeing to West Germany.
                    [0-24099] superscript
                      [0-24100] link: [16]
                        [0-24101] span
                          [0-19031] StaticText: [
                          [0-19032] StaticText: 16
                          [0-19033] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19034] StaticText: On 4 November, the
                    [0-24104] link: Alexanderplatz demonstration
                    [0-19036] StaticText: took place.
                    [0-24105] superscript
                      [0-24106] link: [17]
                        [0-24107] span
                          [0-19037] StaticText: [
                          [0-19038] StaticText: 17
                          [0-19039] StaticText: ]
                  [0-24110] paragraph
                    [0-19040] StaticText: On 6 November, the Interior Ministry published a draft of new travel regulations, which made cosmetic changes to Honecker-era rules, leaving the approval process opaque and maintaining uncertainty regarding access to foreign currency. The draft enraged ordinary citizens, and was denounced as "complete trash" by
                    [0-24111] link: West Berlin Mayor
                    [0-19042] StaticText: 
                    [0-24112] link: Walter Momper
                    [0-19044] StaticText: .
                    [0-24113] superscript
                      [0-24114] link: [18]
                        [0-24115] span
                          [0-19045] StaticText: [
                          [0-19046] StaticText: 18
                          [0-19047] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19048] StaticText: Hundreds of refugees crowded onto the steps of the West German embassy in Prague, enraging the Czechoslovaks, who threatened to seal off the East German–Czechoslovak border.
                    [0-24118] superscript
                      [0-24119] link: [19]
                        [0-24120] span
                          [0-19049] StaticText: [
                          [0-19050] StaticText: 19
                          [0-19051] StaticText: ]
                  [0-24123] paragraph
                    [0-19052] StaticText: On 7 November, Krenz approved the resignation of Prime Minister
                    [0-24124] link: Willi Stoph
                    [0-19054] StaticText: and two-thirds of the Politburo; however, Krenz was unanimously re-elected as General Secretary by the Central Committee.
                    [0-24125] superscript
                      [0-24126] link: [11]
                        [0-24127] span
                          [0-19055] StaticText: [
                          [0-19056] StaticText: 11
                          [0-19057] StaticText: ]
                    [0-24130] superscript
                      [0-24131] span
                        [0-19058] StaticText: :
                        [0-19059] StaticText: 
                        [0-19060] StaticText: 341
                        [0-19061] StaticText: 
                [0-24135] region: New East German emigration policy
                  [0-24136] div
                    [0-24137] heading: New East German emigration policy
                    [0-24140] link: edit
                  [0-24143] paragraph
                    [0-19066] StaticText: On 19 October, Krenz asked
                    [0-24144] link: Gerhard Lauter
                    [0-19068] StaticText: to draft a new travel policy.
                    [0-24145] superscript
                      [0-24146] link: [20]
                        [0-24147] span
                          [0-19069] StaticText: [
                          [0-19070] StaticText: 20
                          [0-19071] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19072] StaticText: Lauter was a former
                    [0-24150] link: People's Police
                    [0-19074] StaticText: officer. After rising rapidly through the ranks, he had recently been promoted to a position with the
                    [0-24151] link: Interior Ministry ("Home Office" / "Department of the Interior")
                    [0-19078] StaticText: as head of the department responsible for issuing passports and the registration of citizens.
                    [0-24153] superscript
                      [0-24154] link: [21]
                        [0-24155] span
                          [0-19079] StaticText: [
                          [0-19080] StaticText: 21
                          [0-19081] StaticText: ]
                  [0-24158] paragraph
                    [0-19082] StaticText: On 8 November, the East German
                    [0-24159] link: Politburo
                    [0-19084] StaticText: enacted a portion of the draft travel regulations addressing
                    [0-19085] StaticText: permanent departure
                    [0-19086] StaticText: immediately. Initially, the Politburo planned to create a special border crossing near
                    [0-24161] link: Schirnding
                    [0-19088] StaticText: specifically for this emigration.
                    [0-24162] superscript
                      [0-23077] link: [22]
                        [0-24163] span
                          [0-19089] StaticText: [
                          [0-19090] StaticText: 22
                          [0-19091] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19092] StaticText: However,
                    [0-24166] link: Interior Ministry officials
                    [0-19094] StaticText: and
                    [0-24167] link: Stasi
                    [0-19096] StaticText: bureaucrats charged with drafting the new text concluded the proposal was not feasible, and instead crafted new text relating to both emigration and temporary travel. The revised text stipulated East German citizens could apply for permission to travel abroad, without having to meet the previous requirements for those trips.
                    [0-24168] superscript
                      [0-24169] link: [23]
                        [0-24170] span
                          [0-19097] StaticText: [
                          [0-19098] StaticText: 23
                          [0-19099] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19100] StaticText: To ease the difficulties, the Krenz-led Politburo decided on 9 November refugees could exit directly through crossing points between East Germany and West Germany, including between East and West Berlin. Later the same day, the ministerial administration modified the proposal to include private, round-trip, travel. The new regulations would take effect the next day.
                    [0-24173] superscript
                      [0-24174] link: [24]
                        [0-24175] span
                          [0-19101] StaticText: [
                          [0-19102] StaticText: 24
                          [0-19103] StaticText: ]

              [0-24260] region: Events
                [0-24261] div
                  [0-24262] heading: Events
                  [0-24265] link: edit
                [0-24268] region: Misinformed public announcements
                  [0-24269] div
                    [0-24270] heading: Misinformed public announcements
                    [0-24273] link: edit
                  [0-24276] figure
                    [0-24277] link
                      [0-23064] image
                    [0-24278] Figcaption
                      [0-19172] StaticText: The press conference on 9 November 1989 by Günter Schabowski (seated on stage, second from right) and other East German officials which led to the fall of the Wall. Riccardo Ehrman is sitting on the floor of the podium with the table just behind him.
                      [0-24279] superscript
                        [0-24280] link: [1]
                          [0-24281] span
                            [0-19173] StaticText: [
                            [0-19174] StaticText: 1
                            [0-19175] StaticText: ]
                  [0-24284] paragraph
                    [0-19176] StaticText: The announcement of the regulations which brought down the Wall took place at an hour-long press conference led by
                    [0-24285] link: Günter Schabowski
                    [0-19178] StaticText: , the outgoing party leader in East Berlin and top party spokesman as Secretary for Information, beginning at 18:00 CET on 9 November and broadcast live on
                    [0-24286] link: East German television
                    [0-19180] StaticText: and
                    [0-24287] link: radio
                    [0-19182] StaticText: . Schabowski was joined by Minister of Foreign Trade
                    [0-24288] link: Gerhard Beil
                    [0-19184] StaticText: and
                    [0-24289] link: Central Committee
                    [0-19186] StaticText: members
                    [0-24290] link: Helga Labs
                    [0-19188] StaticText: and
                    [0-24291] link: Manfred Banaschak
                    [0-19190] StaticText: .
                    [0-24292] superscript
                      [0-24293] link: [1]
                        [0-24294] span
                          [0-19191] StaticText: [
                          [0-19192] StaticText: 1
                          [0-19193] StaticText: ]
                    [0-24297] superscript
                      [0-24298] link: [11]
                        [0-24299] span
                          [0-19194] StaticText: [
                          [0-19195] StaticText: 11
                          [0-19196] StaticText: ]
                    [0-24302] superscript
                      [0-24303] span
                        [0-19197] StaticText: :
                        [0-19198] StaticText: 
                        [0-19199] StaticText: 352
                        [0-19200] StaticText: 
                  [0-24307] paragraph
                    [0-19201] StaticText: Topics of the press conference included the results of votes at the Central Committee meeting, the surprising removal of SED Bezirk First Secretaries
                    [0-24308] link: Hans-Joachim Böhme
                    [0-19203] StaticText: and
                    [0-24309] link: Werner Walde
                    [0-19205] StaticText: , the SED's electoral and press reform plans and the new travel regulations.
                  [0-24310] paragraph
                    [0-19206] StaticText: Schabowski had not been involved in the discussions about the new regulations and had not been fully updated.
                    [0-24311] superscript
                      [0-24312] link: [27]
                        [0-24313] span
                          [0-19207] StaticText: [
                          [0-19208] StaticText: 27
                          [0-19209] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19210] StaticText: Shortly before the press conference, he was handed a note from Krenz announcing the changes, but given no further instructions on how to handle the information. The text stipulated that East German citizens could apply for permission to travel abroad without having to meet the previous requirements for those trips, and also allowed for permanent migration between all border crossings—including those between East and West Berlin.
                    [0-24316] superscript
                      [0-24317] link: [23]
                        [0-24318] span
                          [0-19211] StaticText: [
                          [0-19212] StaticText: 23
                          [0-19213] StaticText: ]
                  [0-24321] paragraph
                    [0-19214] StaticText: At 18:53, near the end of the press conference,
                    [0-24322] link: ANSA
                    [0-19216] StaticText: 's
                    [0-24323] link: Riccardo Ehrman
                    [0-19218] StaticText: asked if the draft travel law of 6 November was a mistake. Schabowski gave a confusing answer that asserted it was necessary because West Germany had exhausted its capacity to accept fleeing East Germans, then remembered the note he had been given and added that a new regulation had been drafted to allow permanent emigration at any border crossing. This caused a stir in the room; amid several questions at once, Schabowski expressed surprise that the reporters had not yet seen this regulation, and started reading from the note.
                    [0-24324] superscript
                      [0-24325] link: [1]
                        [0-24326] span
                          [0-19219] StaticText: [
                          [0-19220] StaticText: 1
                          [0-19221] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19222] StaticText: After this, a reporter, either Ehrman or
                    [0-24330] link: Bild-Zeitung
                    [0-19224] StaticText: reporter Peter Brinkmann, both of whom were sitting in the front row at the press conference,
                    [0-24331] superscript
                      [0-24332] link: [28]
                        [0-24333] span
                          [0-19225] StaticText: [
                          [0-19226] StaticText: 28
                          [0-19227] StaticText: ]
                    [0-24336] superscript
                      [0-24337] link: [29]
                        [0-24338] span
                          [0-19228] StaticText: [
                          [0-19229] StaticText: 29
                          [0-19230] StaticText: ]
                    [0-24341] superscript
                      [0-24342] link: [30]
                        [0-24343] span
                          [0-19231] StaticText: [
                          [0-19232] StaticText: 30
                          [0-19233] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19234] StaticText: asked when the regulations would take effect.
                    [0-24346] superscript
                      [0-24347] link: [1]
                        [0-24348] span
                          [0-19235] StaticText: [
                          [0-19236] StaticText: 1
                          [0-19237] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19238] StaticText: After a few seconds' hesitation, Schabowski replied, "As far as I know, it takes effect immediately, without delay" (
                    [0-24351] link: German
                    [0-19240] StaticText: :
                    [0-24353] i
                      [0-19241] StaticText: Das tritt nach meiner Kenntnis
                      [0-19242] StaticText: 
                      [0-19243] StaticText: ... ist das sofort
                      [0-19244] StaticText: 
                      [0-19245] StaticText: ... unverzüglich
                    [0-19246] StaticText: ).
                    [0-24357] superscript
                      [0-24358] link: [31]
                        [0-24359] span
                          [0-19247] StaticText: [
                          [0-19248] StaticText: 31
                          [0-19249] StaticText: ]
                    [0-24362] superscript
                      [0-24363] link: [32]
                        [0-24364] span
                          [0-19250] StaticText: [
                          [0-19251] StaticText: 32
                          [0-19252] StaticText: ]
                    [0-24367] superscript
                      [0-24368] link: [11]
                        [0-24369] span
                          [0-19253] StaticText: [
                          [0-19254] StaticText: 11
                          [0-19255] StaticText: ]
                    [0-24372] superscript
                      [0-24373] span
                        [0-19256] StaticText: :
                        [0-19257] StaticText: 
                        [0-19258] StaticText: 352
                        [0-19259] StaticText: 
                    [0-19260] StaticText: This was an apparent assumption based on the note's opening paragraph; as Beil attempted to interject that it was up to the
                    [0-24377] link: Council of Ministers
                    [0-19262] StaticText: to decide when it took effect, Schabowski proceeded to read this clause, which stated it was in effect until a law on the matter was passed by the
                    [0-19263] StaticText: Volkskammer
                    [0-19264] StaticText: . Crucially, a journalist then asked if the regulation also applied to the crossings to
                    [0-24379] link: West Berlin
                    [0-19266] StaticText: . Schabowski shrugged and read item 3 of the note, which confirmed that it did.
                    [0-24380] superscript
                      [0-24381] link: [1]
                        [0-24382] span
                          [0-19267] StaticText: [
                          [0-19268] StaticText: 1
                          [0-19269] StaticText: ]
                    [0-24385] superscript
                      [0-24386] link: [29]
                        [0-24387] span
                          [0-19270] StaticText: [
                          [0-19271] StaticText: 29
                          [0-19272] StaticText: ]
                  [0-24390] paragraph
                    [0-19273] StaticText: After this exchange,
                    [0-24391] link: Daniel Johnson
                    [0-19275] StaticText: of
                    [0-24393] link: The Daily Telegraph
                    [0-19277] StaticText: asked what this law meant for the Berlin Wall. Schabowski sat frozen before giving a rambling statement about the Wall being tied to the larger disarmament question.
                    [0-24394] superscript
                      [0-24395] link: [33]
                        [0-24396] span
                          [0-19278] StaticText: [
                          [0-19279] StaticText: 33
                          [0-19280] StaticText: ]
                    [0-24399] superscript
                      [0-24400] link: [28]
                        [0-24401] span
                          [0-19281] StaticText: [
                          [0-19282] StaticText: 28
                          [0-19283] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19284] StaticText: He then ended the press conference promptly at 19:00 as journalists hurried from the room.
                    [0-24404] superscript
                      [0-24405] link: [29]
                        [0-24406] span
                          [0-19285] StaticText: [
                          [0-19286] StaticText: 29
                          [0-19287] StaticText: ]
                    [0-24409] superscript
                      [0-24410] link: [1]
                        [0-24411] span
                          [0-19288] StaticText: [
                          [0-19289] StaticText: 1
                          [0-19290] StaticText: ]
                  [0-24414] paragraph
                    [0-19291] StaticText: After the press conference, Schabowski sat for an interview with
                    [0-24415] link: NBC News
                    [0-19293] StaticText: anchor
                    [0-23076] link: Tom Brokaw
                    [0-19295] StaticText: in which he repeated that East Germans would be able to emigrate through the border and the regulations would go into effect immediately.
                    [0-24416] superscript
                      [0-24417] link: [34]
                        [0-24418] span
                          [0-19296] StaticText: [
                          [0-19297] StaticText: 34
                          [0-19298] StaticText: ]
                    [0-24421] superscript
                      [0-24422] link: [35]
                        [0-24423] span
                          [0-19299] StaticText: [
                          [0-19300] StaticText: 35
                          [0-19301] StaticText: ]
                [0-24426] region: The news spread
                  [0-24427] div
                    [0-24428] heading: The news spread
                    [0-24431] link: edit
                  [0-24434] figure
                    [0-24435] link
                      [0-23065] image
                    [0-24436] Figcaption
                      [0-19306] StaticText: DPA bulletin
                  [0-24437] paragraph
                    [0-19307] StaticText: The news began spreading immediately: the West German
                    [0-24438] link: Deutsche Presse-Agentur
                    [0-19309] StaticText: issued a bulletin at 19:04 which reported that East German citizens would be able to cross the inner German border "immediately". Excerpts from Schabowski's press conference were broadcast on West Germany's two main news programs that night—at 19:17 on
                    [0-24439] link: ZDF
                    [0-19311] StaticText: 's
                    [0-24441] link: heute
                    [0-19313] StaticText: , which came on the air as the press conference was ending, and as the lead story at 20:00 on
                    [0-24442] link: ARD
                    [0-19315] StaticText: 's
                    [0-24444] link: Tagesschau
                    [0-19317] StaticText: . As ARD and ZDF had broadcast to
                    [0-24445] link: nearly all of East Germany
                    [0-19319] StaticText: since the late 1950s, were far more widely viewed than the East German channels, and had become accepted by the East German authorities, this is how most of the population heard the news. Later that night, on ARD's
                    [0-24447] link: Tagesthemen
                    [0-19321] StaticText: , anchorman
                    [0-24448] link: Hanns Joachim Friedrichs
                    [0-19323] StaticText: proclaimed, "This 9 November is a historic day. The GDR has announced that, starting immediately, its borders are open to everyone. The gates in the Wall stand open wide."
                    [0-24449] superscript
                      [0-24450] link: [11]
                        [0-24451] span
                          [0-19324] StaticText: [
                          [0-19325] StaticText: 11
                          [0-19326] StaticText: ]
                    [0-24454] superscript
                      [0-24455] span
                        [0-19327] StaticText: :
                        [0-19328] StaticText: 
                        [0-19329] StaticText: 353
                        [0-19330] StaticText: 
                    [0-24459] superscript
                      [0-24460] link: [27]
                        [0-24461] span
                          [0-19331] StaticText: [
                          [0-19332] StaticText: 27
                          [0-19333] StaticText: ]
                  [0-24464] paragraph
                    [0-19334] StaticText: In 2009, Ehrman claimed that a member of the Central Committee had called him and urged him to ask about the travel law during the press conference, but Schabowski called that absurd.
                    [0-24465] superscript
                      [0-24466] link: [30]
                        [0-24467] span
                          [0-19335] StaticText: [
                          [0-19336] StaticText: 30
                          [0-19337] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19338] StaticText: Ehrman later recanted this statement in a 2014 interview with an Austrian journalist, admitting that the caller was
                    [0-24470] link: Günter Pötschke
                    [0-19340] StaticText: , head of the East German news agency
                    [0-24471] link: ADN
                    [0-19342] StaticText: , and he only asked if Ehrman would attend the press conference.
                    [0-24472] superscript
                      [0-24473] link: [36]
                        [0-24474] span
                          [0-19343] StaticText: [
                          [0-19344] StaticText: 36
                          [0-19345] StaticText: ]
                [0-24477] region: Crowding of the border
                  [0-24478] div
                    [0-24479] heading: Crowding of the border
                    [0-24482] link: edit
                  [0-24485] paragraph
                    [0-19350] StaticText: After hearing the 9 November broadcast, East Germans began gathering at the Wall, at the
                    [0-24486] link: six checkpoints between East and West Berlin
                    [0-19352] StaticText: , demanding that
                    [0-24487] link: border guards
                    [0-19354] StaticText: immediately open the gates.
                    [0-24488] superscript
                      [0-23073] link: [27]
                        [0-24489] span
                          [0-19355] StaticText: [
                          [0-19356] StaticText: 27
                          [0-19357] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19358] StaticText: The surprised and overwhelmed guards made many hectic telephone calls to their superiors about the problem. At first, they were ordered to find the "more aggressive" people gathered at the gates and stamp their passports with a special stamp that barred them from returning to East Germany—in effect, revoking their citizenship. However, this still left thousands of people demanding to be let through "as Schabowski said we can".
                    [0-24492] superscript
                      [0-24493] link: [11]
                        [0-24494] span
                          [0-19359] StaticText: [
                          [0-19360] StaticText: 11
                          [0-19361] StaticText: ]
                    [0-24497] superscript
                      [0-24498] span
                        [0-19362] StaticText: :
                        [0-19363] StaticText: 
                        [0-19364] StaticText: 353
                        [0-19365] StaticText: 
                    [0-19366] StaticText: It soon became clear that no one among the East German authorities would take personal responsibility for issuing orders to use lethal force, so the vastly outnumbered soldiers had no way to hold back the huge crowd of East German citizens.
                    [0-24502] link: Mary Elise Sarotte
                    [0-19368] StaticText: in a 2009
                    [0-19369] StaticText: Washington Post
                    [0-19370] StaticText: story characterized the series of events leading to the fall of the Wall as an accident, saying
                    [0-19371] StaticText: "One of the most momentous events of the past century was, in fact, an accident, a semicomical and bureaucratic mistake that owes as much to the Western media as to the tides of history"
                    [0-19372] StaticText: .
                    [0-24505] superscript
                      [0-24506] link: [27]
                        [0-24507] span
                          [0-19373] StaticText: [
                          [0-19374] StaticText: 27
                          [0-19375] StaticText: ]
                [0-24510] region: Border openings
                  [0-24511] div
                    [0-24512] heading: Border openings
                    [0-24515] link: edit
                  [0-24518] paragraph
                    [0-19380] StaticText: Finally, at 22:45 (alternatively given as 23:30) on 9 November,
                    [0-24519] link: Harald Jäger
                    [0-19382] StaticText: , commander of the
                    [0-24520] link: Bornholmer Straße border crossing
                    [0-19384] StaticText: , yielded, allowing guards to open the checkpoints and let people through with little or no identity-checking.
                    [0-24521] superscript
                      [0-24522] link: [37]
                        [0-24523] span
                          [0-19385] StaticText: [
                          [0-19386] StaticText: 37
                          [0-19387] StaticText: ]
                    [0-24526] superscript
                      [0-24527] link: [38]
                        [0-24528] span
                          [0-19388] StaticText: [
                          [0-19389] StaticText: 38
                          [0-19390] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19391] StaticText: As the
                    [0-24532] link: Ossis
                    [0-19393] StaticText: swarmed through, they were greeted by
                    [0-24534] link: Wessis
                    [0-19395] StaticText: waiting with flowers and champagne amid wild rejoicing. Soon afterward, a crowd of West Berliners jumped on top of the Wall and were soon joined by East German youngsters.
                    [0-24535] superscript
                      [0-24536] link: [39]
                        [0-24537] span
                          [0-19396] StaticText: [
                          [0-19397] StaticText: 39
                          [0-19398] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19399] StaticText: The evening of 9 November 1989 is known as the night the Wall came down.
                    [0-24540] superscript
                      [0-24541] link: [40]
                        [0-24542] span
                          [0-19400] StaticText: [
                          [0-19401] StaticText: 40
                          [0-19402] StaticText: ]
