                    [0-24573] listitem
                      [0-24576] link: The fall of the Wall (November 1989)
                        [0-24577] image: The fall of the Wall (November 1989)
                      [0-19417] StaticText: The fall of the Wall (November 1989)
                    [0-24579] listitem
                      [0-24582] span
                        [0-28989] Video: Unable to play media.
                        [0-28992] button: Play video
                      [0-24675] div
                        [0-19419] StaticText: Celebration at the border crossing in the Schlutup district of
                        [0-24676] link: Lübeck
                  [0-24677] paragraph
                    [0-19421] StaticText: Another border crossing to the south may have been opened earlier. An account by
                    [0-24678] link: Heinz Schäfer
                    [0-19423] StaticText: indicates that he also acted independently and ordered the opening of the gate at Waltersdorf-Rudow a couple of hours earlier.
                    [0-24679] superscript
                      [0-24680] link: [41]
                        [0-24681] span
                          [0-19424] StaticText: [
                          [0-19425] StaticText: 41
                          [0-19426] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19427] StaticText: This may explain reports of East Berliners appearing in West Berlin earlier than the opening of the Bornholmer Straße border crossing.
                    [0-24684] superscript
                      [0-24685] link: [41]
                        [0-24686] span

                          [0-19429] StaticText: 41
                          [0-19430] StaticText: ]
                [0-24689] region: "Wallpeckers" demolition
                  [0-24690] div
                    [0-24691] heading: "Wallpeckers" demolition
                    [0-24695] link: edit
                  [0-24698] figure
                    [0-24699] span
                      [0-29127] Video: Unable to play media.
                      [0-29130] button: Play video
                      [0-29351] StaticText: Duration: 43 seconds.
                    [0-28981] link
                    [0-24792] Figcaption
                      [0-19435] StaticText: A Berlin Wall segment in Los Angeles at 5900 Wilshire Boulevard. 43 second video
                  [0-24793] paragraph
                    [0-19436] StaticText: Removal of the Wall began on the evening of 9 November 1989 and continued over the following days and weeks, with people nicknamed
                    [0-19437] StaticText: Mauerspechte
                    [0-19438] StaticText: (wallpeckers) using various tools to chip off souvenirs, demolishing lengthy parts in the process, and creating several unofficial border crossings.
                    [0-24797] superscript
                      [0-24798] link: [42]
                        [0-24799] span
                          [0-19439] StaticText: [
                          [0-19440] StaticText: 42
                          [0-19441] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19442] StaticText: In the season holidays this became a sort of international action. People from all over the western world went to West Berlin and local youth provided a range of appropriate demolition tools.
                  [0-24802] paragraph
                    [0-19443] StaticText: Television coverage of citizens demolishing sections of the Wall on 9 November was soon followed by the East German regime announcing ten new
                    [0-24803] link: border crossings
                    [0-19445] StaticText: , including the historically significant locations of
                    [0-24804] link: Potsdamer Platz
                    [0-19447] StaticText: ,
                    [0-24805] link: Glienicker Brücke
                    [0-19449] StaticText: , and
                    [0-24806] link: Bernauer Straße
                    [0-19451] StaticText: . Crowds gathered on both sides of the historic crossings waiting for hours to cheer the bulldozers that tore down portions of the Wall to reconnect the divided roads. While the Wall officially remained guarded at a decreasing intensity, new border crossings continued for some time. Initially the
                    [0-24807] link: East German Border Troops
                    [0-19453] StaticText: attempted repairing the damage done by the "wallpeckers"; gradually these attempts ceased, and guards became laxer, tolerating the increasing demolitions and "unauthorized" border crossing through the holes.
                    [0-24808] superscript
                      [0-24809] link: [43]
                        [0-24810] span
                          [0-19454] StaticText: [
                          [0-19455] StaticText: 43
                          [0-19456] StaticText: ]
                [0-24813] region: Prime ministers meet
                  [0-24814] div
                    [0-24815] heading: Prime ministers meet
                    [0-24818] link: edit
                  [0-24821] paragraph
                    [0-19461] StaticText: The
                    [0-24822] link: Brandenburg Gate
                    [0-19463] StaticText: in the Berlin Wall was opened on 22 December 1989; on that date, West German Chancellor
                    [0-24823] link: Helmut Kohl
                    [0-19465] StaticText: walked through the gate and was greeted by East German Prime Minister
                    [0-24824] link: Hans Modrow
                    [0-19467] StaticText: .
                    [0-24825] superscript
                      [0-24826] link: [44]
                        [0-24827] span
                          [0-19468] StaticText: [
                          [0-19469] StaticText: 44
                          [0-19470] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19471] StaticText: West Germans and West Berliners were allowed visa-free travel starting 23 December.
                    [0-24830] superscript
                      [0-24831] link: [43]
                        [0-24832] span
                          [0-19472] StaticText: [
                          [0-19473] StaticText: 43
                          [0-19474] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19475] StaticText: Until then, they could only visit East Germany and East Berlin under restrictive conditions that involved application for a visa several days or weeks in advance and obligatory exchange of at least 25
                    [0-24835] link: DM
                    [0-19477] StaticText: per day of their planned stay, all of which hindered spontaneous visits. Thus, in the weeks between 9 November and 23 December, East Germans could actually travel more freely than Westerners.
                    [0-24836] superscript
                      [0-24837] link: [43]
                        [0-24838] span
                          [0-19478] StaticText: [
                          [0-19479] StaticText: 43
                          [0-19480] StaticText: ]
                [0-24841] region: Official demolition
                  [0-24842] div
                    [0-24843] heading: Official demolition
                    [0-24846] link: edit
                  [0-24849] paragraph
                    [0-19485] StaticText: On 13 June 1990, the East German Border Troops officially began dismantling the Wall,
                    [0-24850] superscript
                      [0-24851] link: [45]
                        [0-24852] span
                          [0-19486] StaticText: [
                          [0-19487] StaticText: 45
                          [0-19488] StaticText: ]
                    [0-24855] superscript
                      [0-24856] link: [46]
                        [0-24857] span
                          [0-19489] StaticText: [
                          [0-19490] StaticText: 46
                          [0-19491] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19492] StaticText: beginning in
                    [0-24860] link: Bernauer Straße
                    [0-19494] StaticText: and around the Mitte district. From there, demolition continued through Prenzlauer Berg/Gesundbrunnen, Heiligensee and throughout the city of Berlin until December 1990. According to estimates by the border troops, a total of around 1.7
                    [0-19495] StaticText: 
                    [0-19496] StaticText: million tonnes of building rubble was produced by the demolition. Unofficially, the demolition of the Bornholmer Straße crossing began because of construction work on the railway. This involved a total of 300 GDR border guards and—after 3 October 1990—600 Pioneers of the Bundeswehr. These were equipped with 175 trucks, 65 cranes, 55 excavators and 13 bulldozers. Virtually every road that was severed by the Berlin Wall, every road that once linked from West Berlin to East Berlin, was reconstructed and reopened by 1 August 1990. In Berlin alone,
                    [0-19497] StaticText: 184
                    [0-19498] StaticText: 
                    [0-19499] StaticText: km (114
                    [0-19500] StaticText: 
                    [0-19501] StaticText: mi)
                    [0-19502] StaticText: of wall,
                    [0-19503] StaticText: 154
                    [0-19504] StaticText: 
                    [0-19505] StaticText: km (96
                    [0-19506] StaticText: 
                    [0-19507] StaticText: mi)
                    [0-19508] StaticText: border fence,
                    [0-19509] StaticText: 144
                    [0-19510] StaticText: 
                    [0-19511] StaticText: km (89
                    [0-19512] StaticText: 
                    [0-19513] StaticText: mi)
                    [0-19514] StaticText: signal systems and
                    [0-19515] StaticText: 87
                    [0-19516] StaticText: 
                    [0-19517] StaticText: km (54
                    [0-19518] StaticText: 
                    [0-19519] StaticText: mi)
                    [0-19520] StaticText: barrier ditches were removed. What remained were six sections that were to be preserved as a memorial. Various military units dismantled the Berlin/Brandenburg border wall, completing the job in November 1991. Painted wall segments with artistically valuable motifs were put up for auction in 1990 in
                    [0-24882] link: Berlin
                    [0-19522] StaticText: and
                    [0-24883] link: Monte Carlo
                    [0-19524] StaticText: .
                    [0-24884] superscript
                      [0-24885] link: [43]
                        [0-24886] span
                          [0-19525] StaticText: [
                          [0-19526] StaticText: 43
                          [0-19527] StaticText: ]
                  [0-24889] paragraph
                    [0-19528] StaticText: On 1 July 1990, the day East Germany adopted the
                    [0-24890] link: West German currency
                    [0-19530] StaticText: , all
                    [0-19531] StaticText: de jure
                    [0-19532] StaticText: border controls ceased, although the inter-German border had become meaningless for some time before that.
                    [0-24892] superscript
                      [0-24893] link: [47]
                        [0-24894] span
                          [0-19533] StaticText: [
                          [0-19534] StaticText: 47
                          [0-19535] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19536] StaticText: The demolition of the Wall was completed in 1994.
                    [0-24897] superscript
                      [0-24898] link: [45]
                        [0-24899] span
                          [0-19537] StaticText: [
                          [0-19538] StaticText: 45
                          [0-19539] StaticText: ]
                  [0-24902] paragraph
                    [0-19540] StaticText: The fall of the Wall marked the first critical step towards
                    [0-24903] link: German reunification
                    [0-19542] StaticText: , which formally concluded a mere 339 days later on 3 October 1990 with the dissolution of East Germany and the official reunification of the German state along the democratic lines of the West German
                    [0-24904] link: Basic Law
                    [0-19544] StaticText: .

                      [0-24906] link: [42]

                [0-24949] region: International opposition
                  [0-24950] div
                    [0-24951] heading: International opposition
                    [0-24954] link: edit
                  [0-24957] paragraph
                    [0-24958] link: French President
                    [0-19569] StaticText: 
                    [0-24959] link: François Mitterrand
                    [0-19571] StaticText: and British Prime Minister
                    [0-24960] link: Margaret Thatcher
                    [0-19573] StaticText: both opposed the eventual reunification of Germany, fearing potential German designs on its neighbours using its increased strength. In September 1989, Margaret Thatcher privately confided to
                    [0-24961] link: Soviet General Secretary
                    [0-19575] StaticText: 
                    [0-24962] link: Mikhail Gorbachev
                    [0-19577] StaticText: that she wanted the Soviet leader to do what he could to stop it.
                    [0-24963] superscript
                      [0-24964] link: [48]
                        [0-24965] span
                          [0-19578] StaticText: [
                          [0-19579] StaticText: 48
                          [0-19580] StaticText: ]
                    [0-24968] superscript
                      [0-24969] link: [49]
                        [0-24970] span
                          [0-19581] StaticText: [
                          [0-19582] StaticText: 49
                          [0-19583] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19584] StaticText: Thatcher told Gorbachev:
                  [0-24974] blockquote
                    [0-24975] paragraph
                      [0-19585] StaticText: We do not want a united Germany. This would lead to a change to postwar borders and we cannot allow that because such a development would undermine the stability of the whole international situation and could endanger our security.
                      [0-24976] superscript
                        [0-24977] link: [48]
                          [0-24978] span
                            [0-19586] StaticText: [
                            [0-19587] StaticText: 48
                            [0-19588] StaticText: ]
                  [0-24981] paragraph
                    [0-19589] StaticText: After the fall of the Berlin Wall, Mitterrand warned Thatcher that a unified Germany could make more ground than
                    [0-24982] link: Adolf Hitler
                    [0-19591] StaticText: ever had and that Europe would have to bear the consequences.
                    [0-24983] superscript
                      [0-24984] link: [50]
                        [0-24985] span
                          [0-19592] StaticText: [
                          [0-19593] StaticText: 50
                          [0-19594] StaticText: ]
              [0-24988] region: Legacy
                [0-24989] div
                  [0-24990] heading: Legacy
                  [0-24993] link: edit
                [0-24996] region: Celebrations and anniversaries
                  [0-24997] div
                    [0-24998] heading: Celebrations and anniversaries
                    [0-25001] link: edit
                  [0-25004] paragraph
                    [0-19603] StaticText: On 21 November 1989,
                    [0-25005] link: Crosby, Stills & Nash
                    [0-19605] StaticText: performed the song "Chippin' Away" from
                    [0-25006] link: Graham Nash
                    [0-19607] StaticText: 's 1986 solo album
                    [0-25008] link: Innocent Eyes
                    [0-19609] StaticText: in front of the Brandenburg Gate.
                    [0-25009] superscript
                      [0-25010] link: [51]
                        [0-25011] span
                          [0-19610] StaticText: [
                          [0-19611] StaticText: 51
                          [0-19612] StaticText: ]
                  [0-25014] paragraph
                    [0-19613] StaticText: On 25 December 1989,
                    [0-25015] link: Leonard Bernstein
                    [0-19615] StaticText: gave a concert in Berlin celebrating the end of the Wall, including
                    [0-25016] link: Beethoven's
                    [0-19617] StaticText: 
                    [0-25017] link: 9th symphony
                    [0-19619] StaticText: (
                    [0-25019] link: Ode to Joy
                    [0-19621] StaticText: ) with the word "Joy"
                    [0-25020] i
                      [0-19622] StaticText: (
                      [0-19623] StaticText: Freude
                      [0-19624] StaticText: )
                    [0-19625] StaticText: changed to "Freedom"
                    [0-25024] i
                      [0-19626] StaticText: (
                      [0-19627] StaticText: Freiheit
                      [0-19628] StaticText: )
                    [0-19629] StaticText: in the lyrics sung. The poet
                    [0-25028] link: Schiller
                    [0-19631] StaticText: may have originally written "Freedom" and changed it to "Joy" out of fear. The orchestra and choir were drawn from both East and West Germany, as well as the United Kingdom, France, the Soviet Union, and the United States.
                    [0-25029] superscript
                      [0-25030] link: [52]
                        [0-25031] span
                          [0-19632] StaticText: [
                          [0-19633] StaticText: 52
                          [0-19634] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19635] StaticText: On New Year's Eve 1989,
                    [0-25034] link: David Hasselhoff
                    [0-19637] StaticText: performed his song "
                    [0-25035] link: Looking for Freedom
                    [0-19639] StaticText: " while standing atop the partly demolished Wall in front of 200,000 people.
                    [0-25036] superscript
                      [0-25037] link: [53]
                        [0-25038] span
                          [0-19640] StaticText: [
                          [0-19641] StaticText: 53
                          [0-19642] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19643] StaticText: 
                    [0-25041] link: Roger Waters
                    [0-19645] StaticText: 
                    [0-25042] link: performed
                    [0-19647] StaticText: the
                    [0-25043] link: Pink Floyd
                    [0-19649] StaticText: album
                    [0-25045] link: The Wall
                    [0-19651] StaticText: just north of
                    [0-25046] link: Potsdamer Platz
                    [0-19653] StaticText: on 21 July 1990, with guests including
                    [0-25047] link: Scorpions
                    [0-19655] StaticText: ,
                    [0-25048] link: Bryan Adams
                    [0-19657] StaticText: ,
                    [0-25049] link: Sinéad O'Connor
                    [0-19659] StaticText: ,
                    [0-25050] link: Cyndi Lauper
                    [0-19661] StaticText: ,
                    [0-25051] link: Thomas Dolby
                    [0-19663] StaticText: ,
                    [0-25052] link: Joni Mitchell
                    [0-19665] StaticText: ,
                    [0-25053] link: Marianne Faithfull
                    [0-19667] StaticText: ,
                    [0-25054] link: Levon Helm
                    [0-19669] StaticText: ,
                    [0-25055] link: Rick Danko
                    [0-19671] StaticText: and
                    [0-25056] link: Van Morrison
                    [0-19673] StaticText: .
                    [0-25057] superscript
                      [0-25058] link: [54]
                        [0-25059] span
                          [0-19674] StaticText: [
                          [0-19675] StaticText: 54
                          [0-19676] StaticText: ]
                  [0-25062] paragraph
                    [0-19677] StaticText: Over the years, there has been a repeated controversial debate
                    [0-25063] superscript
                      [0-25064] link: [55]
                        [0-25065] span
                          [0-19678] StaticText: [
                          [0-19679] StaticText: 55
                          [0-19680] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19681] StaticText: as to whether
                    [0-25068] link: 9 November
                    [0-19683] StaticText: would make a suitable German national holiday, often initiated by former members of political opposition in East Germany, such as
                    [0-25069] link: Werner Schulz
                    [0-19685] StaticText: .
                    [0-25070] superscript
                      [0-25071] link: [56]
                        [0-25072] span
                          [0-19686] StaticText: [
                          [0-19687] StaticText: 56
                          [0-19688] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19689] StaticText: Besides being the emotional apogee of East Germany's peaceful revolution, 9 November is also the date of the 1918 abdication of Kaiser
                    [0-25075] link: Wilhelm II
                    [0-19691] StaticText: and declaration of the
                    [0-25076] link: Weimar Republic
                    [0-19693] StaticText: , the first German republic. However, 9 November is also the anniversary of the execution of
                    [0-25077] link: Robert Blum
                    [0-19695] StaticText: following the
                    [0-25078] link: 1848 Vienna revolts
                    [0-19697] StaticText: , the 1923
                    [0-25079] link: Beer Hall Putsch
                    [0-19699] StaticText: , and the infamous
                    [0-25081] link: Kristallnacht
                    [0-19701] StaticText: 
                    [0-25082] link: pogroms
                    [0-19703] StaticText: of the Nazis in 1938.
                    [0-25083] link: Nobel
                    [0-19705] StaticText: Laureate
                    [0-25084] link: Elie Wiesel
                    [0-19707] StaticText: criticised the first euphoria, noting that "they forgot that 9 November has already entered into history—51 years earlier it marked the Kristallnacht."
                    [0-25085] superscript
                      [0-25086] link: [57]
                        [0-25087] span
                          [0-19708] StaticText: [
                          [0-19709] StaticText: 57
                          [0-19710] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19711] StaticText: As reunification was not official and complete until 3 October (1990), that day was finally chosen as
                    [0-25090] link: German Unity Day
                    [0-19713] StaticText: .
                  [0-25091] region: 10th anniversary celebrations
                    [0-25092] div
                      [0-25093] heading: 10th anniversary celebrations
                      [0-25096] link: edit
                    [0-25099] paragraph
                      [0-19718] StaticText: On 9 November 1999, the 10th anniversary was observed with a concert and fireworks at the
                      [0-25100] link: Brandenburg Gate
                      [0-19720] StaticText: . Russian cellist
                      [0-25101] link: Mstislav Rostropovich
                      [0-19722] StaticText: played music by
                      [0-25102] link: Johann Sebastian Bach
                      [0-19724] StaticText: , while German rock band
                      [0-25103] link: Scorpions
                      [0-19726] StaticText: performed their 1990 song
                      [0-25105] link: Wind of Change
                      [0-19728] StaticText: . Wreaths were placed for victims shot down when they
                      [0-25106] link: attempted to escape to the west
                      [0-19730] StaticText: , and politicians delivered speeches.
                      [0-25107] superscript
                        [0-25108] link: [58]
                          [0-25109] span
                            [0-19731] StaticText: [
                            [0-19732] StaticText: 58
                            [0-19733] StaticText: ]
                      [0-25112] superscript
                        [0-25113] link: [59]
                          [0-25114] span
                            [0-19734] StaticText: [
                            [0-19735] StaticText: 59
                            [0-19736] StaticText: ]
                  [0-25117] region: 20th anniversary celebrations
                    [0-25118] div
                      [0-25119] heading: 20th anniversary celebrations
                      [0-25122] link: edit
                    [0-25125] paragraph
                      [0-19741] StaticText: On 9 November 2009, Berlin celebrated the 20th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall with a "Festival of Freedom" with dignitaries from around the world in attendance for an evening celebration around the Brandenburg Gate. A high point was when over 1,000 colourfully designed foam domino tiles, each over
                      [0-19742] StaticText: 8 feet (2.4
                      [0-19743] StaticText: 
                      [0-19744] StaticText: m)
                      [0-19745] StaticText: tall, that were stacked along the former route of the Wall in the city center were toppled in stages, converging in front of the Brandenburg Gate.
                      [0-25129] superscript
                        [0-25130] link: [60]
                          [0-25131] span
                            [0-19746] StaticText: [
                            [0-19747] StaticText: 60
                            [0-19748] StaticText: ]
                    [0-25134] paragraph
                      [0-19749] StaticText: A Berlin Twitter Wall was set up to allow Twitter users to post messages commemorating the 20th anniversary. The
                      [0-25135] link: Chinese government
                      [0-19751] StaticText: quickly shut down access to the Twitter Wall after internet users in China began using it to protest the
                      [0-25136] link: Great Firewall
                      [0-19753] StaticText: .
                      [0-25137] superscript
                        [0-25138] link: [61]
                          [0-25139] span
                            [0-19754] StaticText: [
                            [0-19755] StaticText: 61
                            [0-19756] StaticText: ]
                      [0-25142] superscript
                        [0-25143] link: [62]
                          [0-25144] span
                            [0-19757] StaticText: [
                            [0-19758] StaticText: 62
                            [0-19759] StaticText: ]
                      [0-25147] superscript
                        [0-25148] link: [63]
                          [0-25149] span
                            [0-19760] StaticText: [
                            [0-19761] StaticText: 63
                            [0-19762] StaticText: ]
                    [0-25152] paragraph
                      [0-19763] StaticText: In the United States, the German Embassy coordinated a public diplomacy campaign with the motto "Freedom Without Walls", to commemorate the 20th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall. The campaign was focused on promoting awareness of the fall of the Berlin Wall among current college students. Students at over 30 universities participated in "Freedom Without Walls" events in late 2009. First place winner of the Freedom Without Walls Speaking Contest
                      [0-25153] superscript
                        [0-25154] link: [64]
                          [0-25155] span
                            [0-19764] StaticText: [
                            [0-19765] StaticText: 64
                            [0-19766] StaticText: ]
                      [0-19767] StaticText: Robert Cannon received a free trip to Berlin for 2010.
                      [0-25158] superscript
                        [0-25159] link: [65]
                          [0-25160] span
                            [0-19768] StaticText: [
                            [0-19769] StaticText: 65
                            [0-19770] StaticText: ]
                    [0-25163] paragraph
                      [0-19771] StaticText: An international project called
                      [0-19772] StaticText: Mauerreise
                      [0-19773] StaticText: (Journey of the Wall) took place in various countries. Twenty symbolic Wall bricks were sent from Berlin starting in May 2009, with the destinations being Korea, Cyprus, Yemen, and other places where everyday life is characterised by division and border experience. In these places, the bricks would become a blank canvas for artists, intellectuals and young people to tackle the "Wall" phenomenon.
                      [0-25165] superscript
                        [0-25166] link: [66]
                          [0-25167] span
                            [0-19774] StaticText: [
                            [0-19775] StaticText: 66
                            [0-19776] StaticText: ]
                    [0-25170] paragraph
                      [0-19777] StaticText: To commemorate the 20th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall, the 3D online virtual world
                      [0-25172] link: Twinity
                      [0-19779] StaticText: reconstructed a true-to-scale section of the Wall in virtual Berlin.
                      [0-25173] superscript
                        [0-25174] link: [67]
                          [0-25175] span
                            [0-19780] StaticText: [
                            [0-19781] StaticText: 67
                            [0-19782] StaticText: ]
                      [0-19783] StaticText: The
                      [0-25178] link: MTV Europe Music Awards
                      [0-19785] StaticText: , on 5 November, had
                      [0-25179] link: U2
                      [0-19787] StaticText: and
                      [0-25180] link: Tokio Hotel
                      [0-19789] StaticText: perform songs dedicated to and about the Berlin Wall. U2 performed at the Brandenburg Gate, and Tokio Hotel performed "
                      [0-25181] link: World Behind My Wall
                      [0-19791] StaticText: ".
                    [0-25182] paragraph
                      [0-25183] link: Palestinians
                      [0-19793] StaticText: in the town of
                      [0-25184] link: Kalandia
                      [0-19795] StaticText: ,
                      [0-25185] link: West Bank
                      [0-19797] StaticText: , pulled down parts of the
                      [0-25186] link: Israeli West Bank barrier
                      [0-19799] StaticText: , in a demonstration marking the 20th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall.
                      [0-25187] superscript
                        [0-25188] link: [68]
                          [0-25189] span
                            [0-19800] StaticText: [
                            [0-19801] StaticText: 68
                            [0-19802] StaticText: ]
                    [0-25192] paragraph
                      [0-19803] StaticText: The
                      [0-25193] link: International Spy Museum
                      [0-19805] StaticText: in Washington D.C., hosted a
                      [0-25194] link: Trabant
                      [0-19807] StaticText: car rally where 20 Trabants gathered in recognition of the 20th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall. Rides were raffled every half-hour and a Trabant crashed through a Berlin Wall mock up. The Trabant was the East German people's car that many used to leave DDR after the collapse.
                      [0-25195] superscript
                        [0-25196] link: [69]
                          [0-25197] span
                            [0-19808] StaticText: [
                            [0-19809] StaticText: 69
                            [0-19810] StaticText: ]
                      [0-25200] superscript
                        [0-25201] link: [70]
                          [0-25202] span
                            [0-19811] StaticText: [
                            [0-19812] StaticText: 70
                            [0-19813] StaticText: ]
                    [0-25205] paragraph
                      [0-19814] StaticText: The
                      [0-25206] link: Allied Museum
                      [0-19816] StaticText: in the
                      [0-25207] link: Dahlem
                      [0-19818] StaticText: district of Berlin hosted a number of events to mark the 20th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall. The museum held a Special Exhibition entitled "Wall Patrol – The Western Powers and the Berlin Wall 1961–1990" which focused on the daily patrols deployed by the Western powers to observe the situation along the Berlin Wall and the fortifications on the
                      [0-25208] link: GDR
                      [0-19820] StaticText: 
                      [0-25209] link: border
                      [0-19822] StaticText: .
                      [0-25210] superscript
                        [0-25211] link: [71]
                          [0-25212] span
                            [0-19823] StaticText: [
                            [0-19824] StaticText: 71
                            [0-19825] StaticText: ]
                      [0-19826] StaticText: A sheet of "Americans in Berlin" Commemorative
                      [0-25215] link: Cinderella stamps
                      [0-19828] StaticText: designed by
                      [0-25216] link: T.H.E. Hill
                      [0-19830] StaticText: was presented to the Museum by David Guerra, Berlin veteran and webmaster of the site
                      [0-25217] link: www.berlinbrigade.com
                      [0-19832] StaticText: .
                      [0-25218] superscript
                        [0-25219] link: [72]
                          [0-25220] span
                            [0-19833] StaticText: [
                            [0-19834] StaticText: 72
                            [0-19835] StaticText: ]
                  [0-25223] region: 30th anniversary celebrations
                    [0-25224] div
                      [0-25225] heading: 30th anniversary celebrations
                      [0-25228] link: edit
                    [0-25231] paragraph
                      [0-19840] StaticText: Berlin planned a week-long arts festival from 4 to 10 November 2019 and a citywide music festival on 9 November to celebrate the 30th anniversary.
                      [0-25232] superscript
                        [0-25233] link: [73]
                          [0-25234] span
                            [0-19841] StaticText: [
                            [0-19842] StaticText: 73
                            [0-19843] StaticText: ]
                      [0-25237] superscript
                        [0-25238] link: [74]
                          [0-25239] span
                            [0-19844] StaticText: [
                            [0-19845] StaticText: 74
                            [0-19846] StaticText: ]
                      [0-19847] StaticText: On 4 November, outdoor exhibits opened at Alexanderplatz, the Brandenburg Gate, the East Side Gallery, Gethsemane Church, Kurfürstendamm, Schlossplatz, and the former Stasi headquarters in Lichtenberg.
                      [0-25242] superscript
                        [0-25243] link: [74]
                          [0-25244] span
                            [0-19848] StaticText: [
                            [0-19849] StaticText: 74
                            [0-19850] StaticText: ]
                [0-25247] region: Polling
                  [0-25248] div
                    [0-25249] heading: Polling
                    [0-25252] link: edit
                  [0-25257] note
                    [0-19855] StaticText: Further information:
                    [0-25258] link: Ostalgie
                  [0-25259] paragraph
                    [0-19857] StaticText: A small minority still support the wall or even support rebuilding the wall back up. A 2008 poll found that 11% of participants from the former West Berlin and 12% from the former East Berlin said it would be better if the wall was still in place.
                    [0-25260] superscript
                      [0-25261] link: [75]
                        [0-25262] span
                          [0-19858] StaticText: [
                          [0-19859] StaticText: 75
                          [0-19860] StaticText: ]
                  [0-25265] paragraph
                    [0-19861] StaticText: A November 2009 poll found that 12% of Germans said the wall should be rebuilt. The poll also found that in the former
                    [0-25266] link: West German states
                    [0-19863] StaticText: support was at 12% and in the former
                    [0-25267] link: East German states
                    [0-19865] StaticText: it was 13%. A September 2009 poll found 15% of Germans supported a wall, while in the west it was 16% and in the east it was at 10%.
                    [0-25268] superscript
                      [0-25269] link: [76]
                        [0-25270] span
                          [0-19866] StaticText: [
                          [0-19867] StaticText: 76
                          [0-19868] StaticText: ]
                    [0-25273] superscript
                      [0-25274] link: [77]
                        [0-25275] span
                          [0-19869] StaticText: [
                          [0-19870] StaticText: 77
                          [0-19871] StaticText: ]
                  [0-25278] paragraph
                    [0-19872] StaticText: A 2010 poll from Emnid for
                    [0-25280] link: Bild
                    [0-19874] StaticText: found that 24% of West Germans and 23% of East Germans wished for the wall to remain.
                    [0-25281] superscript
                      [0-25282] link: [78]
                        [0-25283] span
                          [0-19875] StaticText: [
                          [0-19876] StaticText: 78
                          [0-19877] StaticText: ]
                    [0-25286] superscript
                      [0-25287] link: [79]
                        [0-25288] span
                          [0-19878] StaticText: [
                          [0-19879] StaticText: 79
                          [0-19880] StaticText: ]
                    [0-25291] superscript
                      [0-25292] link: [80]
                        [0-25293] span
                          [0-19881] StaticText: [
                          [0-19882] StaticText: 80
                          [0-19883] StaticText: ]
                    [0-25296] superscript
                      [0-25297] link: [81]
                        [0-25298] span
                          [0-19884] StaticText: [
                          [0-19885] StaticText: 81
                          [0-19886] StaticText: ]
                  [0-25301] paragraph
                    [0-19887] StaticText: A 2011 poll from
                    [0-25303] link: Berliner Zeitung
                    [0-19889] StaticText: on the 30th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall found that 8% of Berliners opposed the fall, while 87% supported the fall. The poll also found that 28% of
                    [0-25304] link: Alternative for Germany
                    [0-19891] StaticText: (AfD) and 16% of
                    [0-25305] link: Free Democratic Party
                    [0-19893] StaticText: (FDP) supporters supported bringing back the wall.
                    [0-25306] superscript
                      [0-25307] link: [82]
                        [0-25308] span
                          [0-19894] StaticText: [
                          [0-19895] StaticText: 82
                          [0-19896] StaticText: ]
                    [0-19897] StaticText: A 2019 Yougov poll found that 13% of Germans wanted the wall back; in the West support was at 14%, and in the East it was 13%.
                    [0-25311] superscript
                      [0-23068] link: [83]
                        [0-25312] span
                          [0-19898] StaticText: [
                          [0-19899] StaticText: 83
                          [0-19900] StaticText: ]
                  [0-25315] paragraph
                    [0-19901] StaticText: A 2019 poll from
                    [0-25316] link: Forsa
                    [0-19903] StaticText: found 35% of Berliners thought the construction of the wall was not bad, with supporters of
                    [0-25317] link: Die Linke
                    [0-19905] StaticText: at 74%.
                    [0-25318] superscript

input.instruction: Find the UK Prime Minister who was in office on 9 November 1989. From the list of prime ministers, extract the name of the PM whose term covers 9 November 1989, along with their term start and end dates.

result.pm_name: Margaret Thatcher [91] MP for Finchley (1925–2013) Premiership

trajectory.finalAnswer: The task was completed successfully. Using Wikipedia, I confirmed via the "Fall of the Berlin Wall" article that the wall fell on 9 November 1989 (following Günter Schabowski's announcement that East Germans could travel freely, leading to crowds overwhelming the border crossings that night). I then verified via the "List of prime ministers of the United Kingdom" article that Margaret Thatcher's premiership ran from 4 May 1979 to 28 November 1990, meaning she was the sitting UK Prime Minister on 9 November 1989. Both facts are corroborated, as the Berlin Wall article itself references British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher in its discussion of that period.

                        [0-29950] StaticText: 10
                        [0-29951] StaticText: ]
                  [0-29952] StaticText: although the country was not renamed officially until 1927, when
                  [0-36444] link: Stanley Baldwin
                  [0-29954] StaticText: was the serving prime minister.
                  [0-36445] superscript
                    [0-36446] link: [11]
                      [0-36447] span
                        [0-29955] StaticText: [
                        [0-29956] StaticText: 11
                        [0-29957] StaticText: ]
              [0-36451] region: Before the Kingdom of Great Britain
                [0-36452] div
                  [0-36453] heading: Before the Kingdom of Great Britain
                  [0-36456] link: edit
                [0-36459] region: Kingdom of England
                  [0-32194] div
                    [0-36460] heading: Kingdom of England
                    [0-36463] link: edit
                  [0-36466] paragraph
                    [0-29966] StaticText: Before the
                    [0-36467] link: Union of England and Scotland
                    [0-29968] StaticText: in 1707, the
                    [0-36468] link: Treasury
                    [0-29970] StaticText: of
                    [0-36469] link: England
                    [0-29972] StaticText: was led by the
                    [0-36470] link: Lord High Treasurer
                    [0-29974] StaticText: .
                    [0-36471] superscript
                      [0-36472] link: [12]
                        [0-36473] span
                          [0-29975] StaticText: [
                          [0-29976] StaticText: 12
                          [0-29977] StaticText: ]
                    [0-29978] StaticText: By the late
                    [0-36476] link: Tudor period
                    [0-29980] StaticText: , the Lord High Treasurer was regarded as one of the
                    [0-36477] link: Great Officers of State
                    [0-29982] StaticText: ,
                    [0-36478] superscript
                      [0-36479] link: [12]
                        [0-36480] span
                          [0-29983] StaticText: [
                          [0-29984] StaticText: 12
                          [0-29985] StaticText: ]
                    [0-29986] StaticText: and was often (though not always) the dominant figure in government:
                    [0-36483] link: Edward Seymour, 1st Duke of Somerset
                    [0-29988] StaticText: (lord high treasurer, 1547–1549),
                    [0-36484] superscript
                      [0-36485] link: [13]
                        [0-36486] span
                          [0-29989] StaticText: [
                          [0-29990] StaticText: 13
                          [0-29991] StaticText: ]
                    [0-29992] StaticText: served as
                    [0-36489] link: lord protector
                    [0-29994] StaticText: to his young nephew King
                    [0-36490] link: Edward VI
                    [0-29996] StaticText: ;
                    [0-36491] superscript
                      [0-36492] link: [13]
                        [0-36493] span
                          [0-29997] StaticText: [
                          [0-29998] StaticText: 13
                          [0-29999] StaticText: ]
                    [0-30000] StaticText: 
                    [0-36496] link: William Cecil, 1st Baron Burghley
                    [0-30002] StaticText: (lord high treasurer, 1572–1598),
                    [0-36497] superscript
                      [0-36498] link: [14]
                        [0-36499] span
                          [0-30003] StaticText: [
                          [0-30004] StaticText: 14
                          [0-30005] StaticText: ]
                    [0-30006] StaticText: was the
                    [0-36502] link: dominant minister
                    [0-30008] StaticText: to Queen
                    [0-36503] link: Elizabeth I
                    [0-30010] StaticText: ;
                    [0-36504] superscript
                      [0-36505] link: [14]
                        [0-36506] span
                          [0-30011] StaticText: [
                          [0-30012] StaticText: 14
                          [0-30013] StaticText: ]
                    [0-30014] StaticText: Burghley's son
                    [0-36509] link: Robert Cecil, 1st Earl of Salisbury
                    [0-30016] StaticText: , succeeded his father as
                    [0-36510] link: chief minister
                    [0-30018] StaticText: to Elizabeth (1598–1603) and was eventually appointed by King
                    [0-36511] link: James I
                      [0-30019] StaticText: James
                      [0-30020] StaticText: 
                      [0-30021] StaticText: I
                    [0-30022] StaticText: as lord high treasurer (1608–1612).
                    [0-36513] superscript
                      [0-36514] link: [15]
                        [0-36515] span
                          [0-30023] StaticText: [
                          [0-30024] StaticText: 15
                          [0-30025] StaticText: ]
                  [0-36518] paragraph
                    [0-30026] StaticText: By the late
                    [0-36519] link: Stuart period
                    [0-30028] StaticText: , the Treasury was often run not by a single individual (i.e., the lord high treasurer) but by a
                    [0-36520] link: commission
                    [0-30030] StaticText: of
                    [0-36521] link: lords of the Treasury
                    [0-30032] StaticText: ,
                    [0-36522] superscript
                      [0-36523] link: [16]
                        [0-36524] span
                          [0-30033] StaticText: [
                          [0-30034] StaticText: 16
                          [0-30035] StaticText: ]
                    [0-30036] StaticText: led by the
                    [0-36527] link: first lord of the Treasury
                    [0-30038] StaticText: . The last lords high treasurer,
                    [0-36528] link: Sidney Godolphin, 1st Earl of Godolphin
                    [0-30040] StaticText: (1702–1710) and
                    [0-36529] link: Robert Harley, 1st Earl of Oxford
                    [0-30042] StaticText: (1711–1714),
                    [0-36530] superscript
                      [0-36531] link: [17]
                        [0-36532] span
                          [0-30043] StaticText: [
                          [0-30044] StaticText: 17
                          [0-30045] StaticText: ]
                    [0-30046] StaticText: ran the government of
                    [0-36535] link: Queen Anne
                    [0-30048] StaticText: .
                    [0-36536] superscript
                      [0-36537] link: [18]
                        [0-36538] span
                          [0-30049] StaticText: [
                          [0-30050] StaticText: 18
                          [0-30051] StaticText: ]
                [0-36541] region: Kingdom of Scotland
                  [0-36542] div
                    [0-36543] heading: Kingdom of Scotland
                    [0-36546] link: edit
                  [0-36549] paragraph
                    [0-30056] StaticText: The
                    [0-36550] link: Chancellor of Scotland
                    [0-30058] StaticText: was effectively the first minister of the kingdom. His department, the
                    [0-36551] link: chancery
                    [0-30060] StaticText: , was responsible for the
                    [0-36552] link: Great Seal
                    [0-30062] StaticText: , which was needed to process the inheritance of land titles and the confirmation of land transfers. His key responsibility was to preside at meetings of the
                    [0-36553] link: privy council
                    [0-30064] StaticText: , and on those rare occasions he attended, at meetings of the
                    [0-36554] link: court of session
                    [0-30066] StaticText: .
                    [0-36555] superscript
                      [0-36556] link: [19]
                        [0-36557] span
                          [0-30067] StaticText: [
                          [0-30068] StaticText: 19
                          [0-30069] StaticText: ]
                    [0-30070] StaticText: The last Chancellor of Scotland, who ran the government during Queen Anne's reign, was
                    [0-36560] link: James Ogilvy, 1st Earl of Seafield
                    [0-30072] StaticText: .
              [0-36561] region: From 1707 to 1721
                [0-36562] div
                  [0-36563] heading: From 1707 to 1721
                  [0-36566] link: edit
                [0-36569] paragraph
                  [0-30077] StaticText: Following the succession of
                  [0-36570] link: George I
                    [0-30078] StaticText: George
                    [0-30079] StaticText: 
                    [0-30080] StaticText: I
                  [0-30081] StaticText: in 1714, the arrangement of a commission of lords of the Treasury (as opposed to a single lord high treasurer) became permanent.
                  [0-36572] superscript
                    [0-36573] link: [20]
                      [0-36574] span
                        [0-30082] StaticText: [
                        [0-30083] StaticText: 20
                        [0-30084] StaticText: ]
                  [0-30085] StaticText: For the next three years, the government was headed by
                  [0-36577] link: Charles Townshend, 2nd Viscount Townshend
                  [0-30087] StaticText: , who was appointed
                  [0-36578] link: Secretary of State for the Northern Department
                  [0-30089] StaticText: .
                  [0-36579] superscript
                    [0-36580] link: [21]
                      [0-36581] span
                        [0-30090] StaticText: [
                        [0-30091] StaticText: 21
                        [0-30092] StaticText: ]
                  [0-30093] StaticText: Subsequently, Lords
                  [0-36584] link: Stanhope
                  [0-30095] StaticText: and
                  [0-36585] link: Sunderland
                  [0-30097] StaticText: ran the government jointly,
                  [0-36586] superscript
                    [0-36587] link: [22]
                      [0-36588] span
                        [0-30098] StaticText: [
                        [0-30099] StaticText: 22
                        [0-30100] StaticText: ]
                  [0-30101] StaticText: with Stanhope managing foreign affairs and Sunderland domestic.
                  [0-36591] superscript
                    [0-36592] link: [22]
                      [0-36593] span
                        [0-30102] StaticText: [
                        [0-30103] StaticText: 22
                        [0-30104] StaticText: ]
                  [0-30105] StaticText: Stanhope died in February 1721 and Sunderland resigned two months later;
                  [0-36596] superscript
                    [0-36597] link: [22]
                      [0-36598] span
                        [0-30106] StaticText: [
                        [0-30107] StaticText: 22
                        [0-30108] StaticText: ]
                  [0-30109] StaticText: Townshend and
                  [0-36601] link: Robert Walpole
                  [0-30111] StaticText: were then invited to form the next government.
                  [0-36602] superscript
                    [0-36603] link: [23]
                      [0-36604] span
                        [0-30112] StaticText: [
                        [0-30113] StaticText: 23
                        [0-30114] StaticText: ]
                  [0-30115] StaticText: From that point, the holder of the
                  [0-36607] emphasis
                    [0-30116] StaticText: office
                  [0-30117] StaticText: of first lord also usually (albeit unofficially) held the status of prime minister. It was not until the
                  [0-36608] link: Edwardian era
                  [0-30119] StaticText: that the title
                  [0-36609] emphasis
                    [0-36610] link: prime minister
                  [0-30121] StaticText: was constitutionally recognised.
                  [0-36611] superscript
                    [0-36612] link: [24]
                      [0-36613] span
                        [0-30122] StaticText: [
                        [0-30123] StaticText: 24
                        [0-30124] StaticText: ]
                  [0-30125] StaticText: The prime minister still holds the office of first lord by constitutional convention,
                  [0-36616] superscript
                    [0-36617] link: [25]
                      [0-36618] span
                        [0-30126] StaticText: [
                        [0-30127] StaticText: 25
                        [0-30128] StaticText: ]
                  [0-30129] StaticText: the only exceptions being the
                  [0-36621] link: Earl of Chatham
                  [0-30131] StaticText: and the
                  [0-36622] link: Marquess of Salisbury
                  [0-30133] StaticText: .
                  [0-36623] superscript
                    [0-36624] link: [26]
                      [0-36625] span
                        [0-30134] StaticText: [
                        [0-30135] StaticText: 26
                        [0-30136] StaticText: ]
